    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A fresh deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    Sources indicate that the county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    Recent findings suggest that according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The newly introduced lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper mentioned.

    The airline prepares to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano mentioned in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    #111314. Why Delta Air Lines Quietly Added ETOPS Certification To Its Boeing 737-900ERs Even Though They Don't Fly Transatlantic & Pacific Legs

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1484 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Delta Air Lines Quietly Added ETOPS Certification To Its Boeing 737-900ERs Even Though They Don't Fly Transatlantic & Pacific Legs

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1484 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, in 2011, Delta Air Lines announced an order for 100 Boeing 737-900ERs, the largest variant of the 737 family.
    • ETOPS stands for Extended-range Twin-engine Operational Performance Standards (or alternatively, Engines Turn Or Passengers Swim), and ETOPS certification demonstrates that a twin-engine aircraft may safely fly more than 60 minutes from a diversion airfield.
    • Modern twinjets are certified by regulators with an ETOPS type design approval, but this doesn't mean that a specific aircraft is ETOPS-certified.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, in 2011, Delta Air Lines announced an order for 100 Boeing 737-900ERs, the largest variant of the 737 family. It later ordered another 20 units in 2015 and another 10 in 2017, bringing its total to 130, and the airline acquired another 33 second-hand aircraft after COVID. They first started arriving in 2013, and the large, efficient 737-900ER has become a workhorse for Delta's domestic network. The type, however, isn't known for exceptional range and flies only within North America. Yet, these aircraft are certified for ETOPS-180 operations.

    ETOPS stands for Extended-range Twin-engine Operational Performance Standards (or alternatively, Engines Turn Or Passengers Swim), and ETOPS certification demonstrates that a twin-engine aircraft may safely fly more than 60 minutes from a diversion airfield. The number denotes how far the aircraft may fly from an airfield in minutes. Although the 737-900ER does not operate any transoceanic flights, Delta has chosen to maintain ETOPS certification on some of its 737-900ERs, but not all of them.

    Modern twinjets are certified by regulators with an ETOPS type design approval, but this doesn't mean that a specific aircraft is ETOPS-certified. Planes need to be individually approved for ETOPS operations, as the regulator needs to verify that the aircraft features special equipment mandatory for overwater operations and that the airline has procedures in place that comply with ETOPS practices. An airline could even choose to have just one aircraft certified for ETOPS, or it could certify its entire fleet if desired.

    According to recent reports, the ETOPS certification process is expensive, and the extra equipment adds weight to the aircraft. Therefore, airlines generally only certify aircraft with ETOPS if the aircraft will regularly operate overwater flights to make the investment worth it. As an example, all of Delta's widebodies are ETOPS certified, but many of its short-haul aircraft are not. Notably, however, the 737-900ER lacks the range to operate transoceanic routes and is primarily used for domestic services.

    Recent findings suggest that but although the 737-900ER is not generally known for having long range, the aircraft is still capable of operating longer services. This includes transcontinental flights or services to the Caribbean.

    While ETOPS is not generally necessary for Caribbean flights, it can permit more efficient routings in some cases, and the 737-900ER is still commonly deployed on the carrier's routes to this region. In addition, while the role of the 737-900ER has been changing as Delta receives a higher number of newly introduced narrowbody aircraft, the carrier formerly had a majority of its 737-900ERs ETOPS certified.

    Sources indicate that today, Delta only maintains a small subfleet of roughly 20 737-900ERs with ETOPS certification, while the remaining are not certified for extended overwater operations. However, many of these planes formerly featured equipment for ETOPS operations and were maintained to ETOPS-180 standards. Delta later removed the extra equipment from many of its 737s and no longer holds them to ETOPS standards.

    Sources indicate that the 737-900ER was Delta's newest and most economical large narrowbody in the mid-2010s. With such a large order, the Atlanta-based carrier intended to deploy the 737-900ER throughout its network on some of its longest routes within North America. Some of these are Caribbean services that would require ETOPS certification for more efficient routings; hence, most of the 737-900ERs got ETOPS certification. In addition, Delta also originally intended to use the 737-900ER for some of its services to Hawaii from the West Coast, which necessitates ETOPS-180.

    Recent findings suggest that ETOPS equipment and maintaining ETOPS certification for an aircraft is expensive, so Delta has removed it from most 737s as the airline uses the 737 on fewer overwater routes today. Part of this is because the carrier now has a large Airbus A321neo fleet, which has been deployed on longer Caribbean routes due to its excellent fuel efficiency. The other reason is that the previously planned Hawaii services didn't work out, and Delta pulled the 737s from these operations.

    Sources indicate that until the arrival of the 737-900ER, Delta primarily relied on the far less efficient 757 for its routes from the West Coast to Hawaii. In 2016, the airline began scheduling the 737-900ER on flights between Seattle and Honolulu, while the 737 began flying to Kona shortly afterwards. However, the airline would end up pulling the 737-900ER off of these routes, instead replacing it with the 757 again, as these routes pushed the 737-900ER too far past its payload-range limitations.

    The 737-900ER can and has operated longer routes than these Hawaii services, even for Delta itself. However, operating an ETOPS flight requires extra fuel reserves; in the case of the Hawaii routes, the aircraft needs to carry enough fuel to essentially turn around midway and go all the way back after losing an engine, as there are no diversion airports between the West Coast and Hawaii. The fuel reserves add significant weight, cutting into payload, and the 737-900ERs were frequently payload-restricted when flying to Hawaii, hurting revenue.

    In a recent development, united Airlines also faced this same matter when operating the 737-900ER to Hawaii, but the Chicago-based carrier had a smaller 757 fleet than Delta, and most of its examples were configured with lie-flat business class seats. Delta, with its large subfleets of domestic-configured 757s, was able to switch the routes back to the 757s, which cost more to operate but also earned more revenue. Today, Delta mainly relies on the A321neo for its Hawaii routes, while United relies on the 737 MAX, neither of which faces these concerns.

    In a recent development, delta Air Lines uses the A321neo, 737-900ER, and 757 for routes to the Caribbean and Hawaii. Because its network of overwater routes within North America is operated by several types, the airline maintains subfleets of planes with ETOPS certification and planes without. Only about half of the A321neos are certified for ETOPS operations, as well as select 737s and 757s. As a whole, just over 100 of Delta's 828 narrowbodies are certified for ETOPS, because this is all that the airline needs.

    According to recent reports, united Airlines, however, certifies all of its 640 737s and 61 757s for ETOPS operations. The 737s are the airline's primary aircraft for Caribbean and Hawaii routes, while the 757-200 is heavily used to Europe. The 757-300s are also still used on several of United's flights to Hawaii. Still, the carrier has significantly more ETOPS-certified aircraft than it likely needs; it even maintains ETOPS certification on its 12 737-900s, which mainly operate short domestic trips out of Houston. This is a costlier approach, but what it allows is operational flexibility.

    Delta Air Lines Narrowbody Fleet.

    United Airlines Narrowbody Fleet.

    If an ETOPS-certified 737 goes out of service, United can just swap it for another 737 without complicating the rest of its schedule. If one of Delta's ETOPS-certified 737s is taken out of service, the carrier has to swap it out for another ETOPS-certified 737, of which it has far fewer. Delta is maintaining separate subfleets of A321neos, 737s, and 757s, which is a less flexible arrangement regarding operational disruptions and spares. By certifying all of its 737s with ETOPS, United avoids this problem.

    United doesn't maintain ETOPS certification on its A319-100, A320-200, or A321neo fleets, and so it essentially designates one aircraft type (the 737) for Caribbean and Hawaii runs, while the A320 family is restricted to the US mainland. The catch is that this approach is more expensive upfront.

    Sources indicate that ETOPS certification is not generally required for flights from the US to the Caribbean. However, there are some airways southeast of Bermuda to the Eastern Caribbean that take an aircraft more than 60 minutes away from a diversion airfield, and if Bermuda is unavailable as a diversion point, then planes need to hug the Florida coastline. While ETOPS certification is not necessary for Caribbean flights, it does offer benefits through more direct flight paths, and it is necessary for Hawaii operations.

    In a recent development, to actually be certified for ETOPS operations, an aircraft needs to be maintained according to a special ETOPS program. It needs to be equipped with additional communications and navigation equipment, and an ETOPS-qualified mechanic is required to complete a service check before the flight. The engines must be inspected by two separate technicians, and the aircraft's maintenance logs also denote it specifically as being ETOPS-certified.

    ETOPS is meant to be a thorough process that ensures a twinjet can safely fly far away from a diversion point due to having only two engines. Because it's expensive, airlines generally only certify aircraft with ETOPS if the plane will routinely be used on overwater routes. Even if a route doesn't necessarily require it, ETOPS can offer better routings that save time and fuel. Today, 737s and A321s now routinely operate overwater routes to Hawaii or across oceans, and this would have been unimaginable 40 years ago.

    California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

    Sources indicate that but California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

    “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

    Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

    “While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he stated.

    Industry observers note that leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

    BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

    In a recent development, california Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

    In a recent development, working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

    But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

    Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

    Recent findings suggest that “Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

    Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

    “A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

    Sources indicate that several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

    Recent findings suggest that colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

    The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez mentioned. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

    Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

    “The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

    Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.
    • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
    • However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

    As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

    However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

    In a recent development, I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

    Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

    After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

    I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

    Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

    I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

    The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

    Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

    As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and showed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically said, “that means nothing.”.

    So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

    In a recent development, once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

    Industry observers note that only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

    Airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

    Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

    Recent findings suggest that that feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

    For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

    Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

    Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That said, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

    Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

    According to recent reports, even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

    Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

    It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

    Sources indicate that the legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

    In a recent development, it was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

    Sources indicate that as for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

    Industry observers note that imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

    It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of new Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

    It has been revealed that if I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….

    Really? AR is probably the best airline for regional flights in South America. Are you Brazilian Daniel? That would explain it all, however, I´m not sure this Josh Cahill wannabe clickbait style fits OMAAT. Good luck.

    Recent findings suggest that best thing about them: Their livery. Stunning!. In person even better.

    According to recent reports, I flew from GRU to LHR on BA in about 2018, first class redemption. I don't remember a long passport queue, but I do remember that I was escorted by the check-in agent from the desk to the lounge which I found surprising, but could explain the lack of issues. Have the rules changed, or have air France not worked out how to bypass the queue?

    It has been revealed that LATAM is no better. I had to fight tooth and nail with them at AEP over baggage allowances. I finally got a stupervisor and quoted actual tariff rules.     #111310. The True Cost Airbus Charges For An A330neo Compared With Boeing's 787-9 Dreamliner

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1476 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The True Cost Airbus Charges For An A330neo Compared With Boeing's 787-9 Dreamliner

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1476 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Airbus A330-900 (A330neo) and the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner are very close competitors.
    • Industry observers note that as Simple Flying has previously highlighted, headline list figures are an unreliable method to determine the true costs and value of aircraft and aero engines.
    • To understand why list prices are not particularly useful, it is necessary to understand what they are.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Airbus A330-900 (A330neo) and the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner are very close competitors. On the face of it, the 787-9 has a much larger order book (1,493 vs 511), has a noticeably higher market value, and is a cleansheet aircraft. This could be interpreted as suggesting the 787-9 has a cost advantage over the A330-900. However, the truth is more complicated, and it allows the A330-900 to remain competitive.

    Industry observers note that as Simple Flying has previously highlighted, headline list figures are an unreliable method to determine the true costs and value of aircraft and aero engines. To faithfully answer the headline of this article, list prices need to be set aside in favor of market prices and lease rates. The aviation industry runs on very thin margins. Consequently, averaging the costs of these two aircraft without considering the contingent variables of the airline in question will likely provide highly misleading numbers.

    To understand why list prices are not particularly useful, it is necessary to understand what they are. An aircraft manufacturer’s list price is the published, baseline 'sticker price' for a newly introduced aircraft before negotiated discounts, rebates, or custom configuration changes. These are typically inflated prices where the manufacturer is essentially saying, "this is what we value our product at," even though it realistically never sells them at that price and airlines and lessors would never pay it.

    Industry observers note that for an analogy, think of an airline offering the chance to win a holiday package "valued at $10,000." That figure may include estimates for tours, accommodation, flights, transfers, etc., all priced at the highest retail price. In practice, the airline would likely be utilizing spare capacity, receiving bulk discounts, and having special pricing arrangements, so it's only paying a fraction of the headline figure.

    Likewise, holidaymakers may be able to book their own analogous trip at a fraction of the cost. List prices are similar, although they may provide a starting point in complex aircraft negotiations. As discussed below, sometimes the airplane manufacturer (Airbus, Boeing) has significant bargaining power in negotiations, while at other times the balance can swing to the customer (e.g., Emirates vis-à-vis the 777-9).

    It has been revealed that at the moment, the market values for Boeing 787-9s and A330neos are unusually high due to production bottlenecks at Airbus and Boeing. IBA writes, "This has pushed the expected delivery dates for many recent orders as far back as early 2030. With hampered production rates, it comes as no surprise that this has, in turn, allowed for Market Values and MLRs to rally over the years." The value of widebody aircraft has grown especially fast over the last year.

    In a November 2026 update, IBA reported, "Constrained supply is supporting trading values, with 2026 market values up 7% for the 787-9, 5% for the A350-900, 24% for the 777-300ER and 20% for the A330-300, alongside rising lease rates." This demonstrates a significant increase in market value for the older A330-300 cousin to the A330neo, but fails to include the A330neo price increase.

    Cost comparison (per IBA, My Air Trade, Green Airlines).

    Market value (oldest airframes).

    Sources indicate that while it's unclear how much the A330-900's market value has increased recently, its market lease rates are up by as much as 13%. The monthly market lease rate for a new Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is around $1.05-$1.16 million, and around $900,000-$990,000 for the A330neo. At mid-age, the 787-9's rate is around $695,000-$792,000, while the A330neo is around $600,000-$756,000 per month.

    In Q1 2026, for a newly delivered Airbus A330-900, IBA ascribed a market value of $118.5 million. Meanwhile, a new Boeing 787-9 is expected to trade in the region of $160 million. Overall, the new-delivery market value of a Boeing 787-9 is estimated to be in the $151–$160 million range by different industry analysts. The new-delivery market value range of an A330-900 (A330neo) is around $118.5–$119 million.

    In a recent development, for comparison, the market value for larger 787-10 newly introduced-builds is around $168 million, or about $8 million more than the standard 787-9. The new value of the short 787-8 is around $116 million, or almost the same as a new A330-900. My Air Trade indicates that the oldest 787-9 is estimated at around $70.6 million, while the oldest A330-900 is valued at around $73 million.

    The oldest second-hand examples are estimated to be $47 million for the 787-8 and $95 million for the 787-10. No market values are given for the unpopular A330-800 variant, perhaps due to the limited deliveries and lack of market trading for the aircraft. Separately, the market values for the A380 are very low. The oldest A380s are estimated to be worth $12 million, and the most valuable are around $45 million. Put another way, a latest A330-900 is worth around 3x-10x that of the world's remaining A380s.

    The A330-900 and Boeing 787-9 compete on the market for a similar (but not the same) market segment. These aircraft are similar in length and have comparable typical 3-class seating capacities: 260-300 for the A330-900 and 250-290 for the 787-9. The maximum seating is around 460 and 420, respectively. In practice, the 787-9s are typically assigned more to flagship routes than the A330neo and are configured with an average of 264 seats, compared with the A330-900's denser 281-seat average.

    According to recent reports, they have almost identical maximum take-off weights (251 tonnes vs 254 tonnes) and are both very competitive in terms of cargo capacity. The Boeing 787-9 is deemed to have a modest advantage in range, although that only matters in edge cases, as most missions are well within the A330neo's maximum range. When it comes to fuel burn, it depends heavily on payload, configuration, and range. As a rule, the 787-9's fuel advantage grows with longer ranges.

    According to recent reports, one of the biggest differences is that the 787-9 is a fundamentally cleansheet composite aircraft, while the A330neo is a comprehensive upgrade on the 1980s-designed A330. The A330neo has newly introduced engines, new wings, new avionics, and other updates, but it still has an older architecture and a mostly aluminum fuselage.

    It is impossible to put a precise figure on how much the A330-900 and 787-9 cost to operate relative to each other. Too much is contingent. Even setting aside that these aircraft are better optimized for different routes and missions, many airline-specific factors matter. One crucial factor is the composition of the airline's overall fleet.

    If an airline (e.g., Delta) also operates older A330s and new A350s, it can significantly increase fleet commonality and significantly reduce maintenance and training expenses. Airbus claims up to 95% commonality in A330ceo/A330neo spare parts, including substantial tooling commonality and the same pilot type rating between the generations. Airbus also claims, "Today, the A321neo and the A330neo have proven to deliver up to 30% lower operating costs when operated together.".

    In a recent development, by contrast, the benefits of commonality are more limited with airlines operating the Boeing 777 and Boeing 787, with no common type rating and the 787 requiring dedicated tooling. Commonality with the predecessor Boeing 767 is even more limited. However, there is a very high benefit to operating parallel fleets of 787-8s and 787-10s. The value of commonality can drive major airlines (e.g., Southwest, Ryanair) to only operate one family of aircraft.

    According to recent reports, as shown by the market prices, the A330-900 is around $30–40 million cheaper in upcoming aircraft value and has a lower lease rate per month. This suggests the A330-900 benefits from lower capital, financing, and leasing costs. But this hides a major distortion. This is the secondary-market value, not the cost at which they were purchased. The largest order (cumulative) for the A330-900 is by Cathay Pacific for 41, while the largest cumulative order for the 787-9 is 132 by United (and 221 for all Boeing 787 variants).

    As a general rule, an airline purchasing aircraft in the single digits may be in a negotiating position to get around 25% off the list price (with massive variation). An airline ordering 50–100 aircraft could be able to negotiate a 45–55% discount off the list price. These purchase price differences disappear once they hit the secondary market.

    In practice, airlines can bundle orders, as when Qatar Airways ordered 130 Dreamliners and 30 Boeing 777-9s with options for 50 Boeing 787/777X airliners. All this is to say that the cost of operating an A330-900 may be higher or lower than that of the 787-9, depending on the circumstances. Using some back-of-the-envelope math, both airliners will likely cost around $13,000 per flight hour to operate, plus or minus a few thousand dollars. The winner will be highly contingent.

    End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that american Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore.
    • As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.
    • Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that american Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

    As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

    Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with new cabins, including the new business class.

    Still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

    Industry observers note that with this change, no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore either, so it very much is the end of an era. American’s 777 first class seats were controversial — on the one hand, I kind of love how they swivel, though on the other hand, they really lack privacy, and the soft product left a lot to be desired.

    Industry observers note that I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

    It’s great that these planes will be getting new business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

    While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

    Specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between Newly introduced York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

    American also intends to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

    According to recent reports, american has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

    In a recent development, american Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and upcoming business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

    In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

    #111307. Why Airlines Accept The Airbus A321XLR's Heavier 101.5-Tonne Maximum Takeoff Weight On Flights Shorter Than An Hour

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1581 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Airlines Accept The Airbus A321XLR's Heavier 101.5-Tonne Maximum Takeoff Weight On Flights Shorter Than An Hour

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Airbus A321XLR has helped open a new chapter in long-and-thin aviation.
    • In a recent development, despite its impressive capabilities, airlines have been known to put the XLR to work on connections that span a fraction of the distance the aircraft can actually fly.
    • On the surface, the A321XLR and standard Airbus A321neo appear almost identical.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Airbus A321XLR has helped open a new chapter in long-and-thin aviation. As the latest variant to appear in the Airbus A320 family, the XLR — or Extra Long Range — has taken the crown as the longest-range commercial narrowbody. Simply put, it has provided operators with arguably the best means yet of efficiently serving long-haul routes that would otherwise be unsuited to larger, widebody aircraft.

    In a recent development, despite its impressive capabilities, airlines have been known to put the XLR to work on connections that span a fraction of the distance the aircraft can actually fly. In some extreme cases, these do not even stretch to an hour of flight time. But modifications were needed for the XLR to earn its title, and these added weight. So for those opting to schedule their XLRs on such short routes, the reality is accepting the penalties of operating a heavier plane than might normally do the job. Nonetheless, carriers continue to do so anyway, which raises the question: Why?

    On the surface, the A321XLR and standard Airbus A321neo appear almost identical. They share a score of common features, from their engines to their capacities to their basic dimensions, including wingspans and the same fuselage length, width, and height. A bystander could not be blamed for mistaking one for the other as a result.

    Sources indicate that airbus deliberately developed the duo this way too, with these retained features making it operationally viable for airlines to operate both variants in their fleets. Unchanged dimensions mean the same gate spacing and ground equipment can be used at airports, for instance. It also simplifies crew training, as pilots can fly either variant without having to train for an entirely separate type rating.

    Select A321XLR and A321neo specifications, from Airbus:.

    4,700 nautical miles (8,700 km).

    4,000 nautical miles (7,400 km).

    146 feet, 0 inches (44.51 meters).

    146 feet, 0 inches (44.51 meters).

    117 feet, 5 inches (35.80 meters).

    117 feet, 5 inches (35.80 meters).

    38 feet, 8 inches (11.76 meters).

    38 feet, 8 inches (11.76 meters).

    CFM LEAP-1A / Pratt & Whitney PW1100G.

    CFM LEAP-1A / Pratt & Whitney PW1100G.

    There are key differences between the two, which is why the XLR has a stronger range and higher maximum takeoff weight. The range is largely enabled by the addition of a permanent 3,407.82-US gallon (12,900-3liter) rear center tank on the XLR, which also explains the increased weight; Airbus has also developed an updated fuel system and outfitted the variant with necessary structural reinforcements. Ultimately, this has pushed the XLR’s maximum range to 4,700 nautical miles (8,700 km) — which is a notable step up on the NEO’s.

    It has been revealed that because of this, any instance where an airline chooses to use the A321XLR on a short-haul hop may seem counterintuitive. Indeed, the XLR was specifically designed to increase the A320 family's top range. Even so, many airlines do use the variant for this purpose in practice.

    In a recent development, air Canada uses its XLRs in part to connect Ottawa Macdonald-Cartier International Airport (YOW) and Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ), as well as Montréal-Trudeau International Airport (YUL) and Toronto, for instance. Each of these journeys lasts roughly 39 and 53 minutes, respectively, spanning between 197 nautical miles (364 km) and 274 nautical miles (507 km). Concurrently, the carrier also services its almost nine-hour Toronto to Tenerife South Airport (TFS) route using XLRs.

    Across the Atlantic, Ireland’s Aer Lingus XLRs flew more than 300 flights exceeding 3,100 miles (2,694 nautical miles or 4,989 km), alongside over 200 flights of 1,250 miles (1,086 nautical miles or 2,012 km) or fewer, in July this year, according to aviation data platform Avi-Go. These included Dublin Airport (DUB) to Nashville International Airport (BNA), scheduled at nine hours and 20 minutes, but also Dublin to London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and Dublin to Josep Tarradellas Barcelona–El Prat Airport (BCN), lasting just 48 minutes and one hour and 50 minutes, respectively. Needless to say, the XLR is by no means solely used for its range in either case.

    Sources indicate that air Canada and Aer Lingus are not alone, though. It is common practice among A321XLR operators to run the models on diverse routes with wide-ranging flight times and distances. At least, this is the case as it stands.

    Based on data from aviation analyst Cirium covering last July, American Airlines, Saudia, and Wizz Air were among the handful of XLR operators that were doing just that. The former flew its XLRs on journeys spanning the 540- to 1,079-nautical mile (1,000- to 1,999-km) and 2,700 to 3,239-nautical mile (5,000- to 5,999-km) brackets, as well as everything in between. Interestingly, these figures indicated Iberia — the XLR’s launch customer back in October 2024 — was the only carrier to exclusively use the variant for connections in the highest 2,700- to 3,239-nautical mile (5,000- to 5,999-km) and 3,240- to 3,779-nautical mile (6,000- to 6,999-km) brackets over the course of the month.

    Airbus A321XLR operators as of mid-November:.

    According to recent reports, in other words, the carrier that has had the most time to incorporate the aircraft into its fleet appeared to be the one getting the most out of the XLR’s range most frequently. That is not surprising, though, given Airbus has only begun delivering the model in the past few years. By our count, just 61 models had been delivered to 11 carriers as of the time of writing in November, out of more than 500 orders placed.

    Recent findings suggest that as such, those tasked with fitting the A321XLR into wider schedules have only recently benefited from the jets actually being on hand. Although orders placed years in advance will have given time to prepare, there is little replacement for real-world experience — especially since the XLR is, in many ways, unmatched by anything that has come before it.

    In a recent development, in Iberia’s case, the XLR has appeared more capable than anticipated. “[It’s] even better than originally planned in terms of stage length,” chief executive Marco Antonio Trujillo remarked previously. “In fact, we are operating currently to the Caribbean, San Juan and Santo Domingo, where initially we were not thinking that the range could get over there.”.

    Industry observers note that on the flip side, Air Canada had planned to introduce XLRs between Toronto and London Heathrow this year. However, the Canadian flag carrier pulled the type before it could even debut on the service, instead opting to stick with narrowbodies for the time being. All of this goes to say, planning in advance is one thing, but meeting operational requirements in real time can be another story altogether.

    This can also explain why widebodies are sometimes used for surprisingly short journeys. Where the A321XLR’s capacity makes it an ideal, like-for-like replacement for other narrowbodies and the A321neo in particular, sometimes that is not even enough.

    Several short-haul services this year were scheduled to be flown by widebodies, as flagged by industry publication Aerospace Global News, which are traditionally associated with long-haul routes. Not least, the Airbus A350 — itself known for carrying out the longest flights on offer today — was deployed on several intra-European flights, as shown below. Similarly, the double-decker Airbus A380 saw use within Asia on a sub-six-hour connection that would technically fail to qualify as long-haul by definition.

    Select widebody-operated short-haul routes scheduled for this year, from Aerospace Global News:.

    Montreal (YUL) — Quebec City (YQB).

    Helsinki (HEL) — London Heathrow (LHR).

    1,001 nautical miles (1,853 km).

    Singapore (SIN) — Shanghai (PVG).

    2,049 nautical miles (3,794 km).

    According to recent reports, as to why such huge aircraft are selected for flights that do not quite match up to their capabilities, there are several reasons. Demand, for example, may call for more seats and make a bigger jet the more viable option. Airport slot constraints may similarly play a part, leaving airlines having to move greater numbers of passengers at once. The same factors apply to the XLR, which is designed to offer carriers a lower-risk alternative when demand isn't there to support running a widebody. No doubt, that also stretches to opening up fresh so-called long and thin routes, although discovering these will take time, as we are seeing today.

    Recent findings suggest that at the core of all the decision-making as to which aircraft to use on which route, when and how often, and so on, is the simple fact that a plane sitting out of action on the ground is a plane not generating revenue. Whether it's a narrowbody or a widebody, using it is better than leaving it idle while waiting for the perfect deployment. Add in factors such as demand, and the reasons an aircraft type may not appear to match the route distance pile up.

    Industry observers note that in the case of the A321XLR, Airbus has created a model as impressive for its flexibility as it is for its range. Yes, it can match several widebodies in distance, replacing them if needed due to lackluster demand. It can also fill in or complement fellow narrowbodies when required, thanks to its commonality with the A321neo.

    The caveat is the weight penalty, which is most noticeable on shorter routes. Nonetheless, airlines have clearly deemed it an acceptable trade-off to keep both their routes and jets active, and thus generating revenue in turn.

In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

    Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their latest A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.
    • I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg.
    • In a recent development, however, to answer the economy vs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their latest A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

    I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

    In a recent development, however, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

    If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

    The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

    Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

    To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

    According to recent reports, it’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

    Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

    Industry observers note that I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

    As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

    After the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and noted she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

    I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

    Sources indicate that in the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

    Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time….

    In a recent development, I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

    If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

    Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

    #111303. Industry News: Why United & American Airlines Are Fighting Over The Future Of Chicago O’Hare

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1671 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Why United & American Airlines Are Fighting Over The Future Of Chicago O’Hare

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), a bitter turf war between United Airlines and American Airlines has escalated from lobbying into courtroom battles, aggressive schedule expansions, and federal intervention.
    • It has been revealed that what makes this showdown more than a routine squabble over airport real estate is how O'Hare's departure-based gate formula, local traveler loyalty, and delayed terminal expansion reshape both carriers' economics.
    • Unlike New York-JFK or LaGuardia airport, where FAA slot rules directly govern takeoffs and landings, gate access at Chicago O'Hare is governed by agreements between airlines and the City of Chicago under its airport use and lease framework.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), a bitter turf war between United Airlines and American Airlines has escalated from lobbying into courtroom battles, aggressive schedule expansions, and federal intervention. Clashes over gate redistributions, including United's late-2025 gains and American's subsequent push to reclaim ground, have turned the airport's concourses into a tense contest between two legacy rivals. At the same time, soaring flight schedules have collided with airfield construction, prompting federal caps to head off gridlock.

    It has been revealed that what makes this showdown more than a routine squabble over airport real estate is how O'Hare's departure-based gate formula, local traveler loyalty, and delayed terminal expansion reshape both carriers' economics. From maneuvering around Spirit Airlines' Concourse G gates to confronting Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) daily flight limits and broader credit-card loyalty stakes, the fight tests just how far two airlines will go to defend or expand their foothold in America's heartland.

    Unlike New York-JFK or LaGuardia airport, where FAA slot rules directly govern takeoffs and landings, gate access at Chicago O'Hare is governed by agreements between airlines and the City of Chicago under its airport use and lease framework. Across O'Hare's four terminals and nearly 200 total gates, airlines lease preferential-use gates alongside common-use facilities that support flights across the airfield. As coverage from Airways Magazine and Travel Weekly explains, holding more preferential gates directly supports larger flight banks, smoother turnarounds, and greater scheduling flexibility at a busy connecting hub.

    Industry observers note that under O'Hare's use-it-or-lose-it allocation mechanism, gate assignments are tied closely to departure share and prior-year flight activity and are not treated as permanent, untouchable real estate. Airlines submit schedules and usage data, allowing the city's Department of Aviation to review activity and redistribute gates annually when utilization shifts. That formula creates a clear mathematical link between flying more flights and expanding or defending concourse space.

    It has been revealed that departure volume carries so much weight in periodic gate redetermination, so the rulebook naturally rewards aggressive scheduling and penalizes carriers that let gates sit idle or pull back capacity. Even small single-digit shifts in gate counts across concourses such as Terminal 3 or Concourse G can alter how tightly an airline packs its banks. In practice, that structure makes every year an overall score marker where schedule discipline and flight volume directly shape future gate real estate.

    Supported by its downtown Chicago headquarters and a leading gate footprint around 95 to 99 gates across O'Hare, United Airlines has treated the hub fight as a line-in-the-sand defense of its Midwestern stronghold, as noted by Reuters. Following late-2025 gate reallocation gains and CEO Scott Kirby's pledge not to lose a single gate at United's expense, the carrier has leaned hard into schedule growth to protect its departure share. Coverage from The Points Guy and CBS Chicago highlights how United rolled out a major 2026 expansion, adding upcoming routes and increasing frequencies across dozens of existing markets, to lock in operational scale.

    That schedule offensive has been paired with an aggressive push to match or fend off rival moves on the ground, including United stepping in to acquire Spirit Airlines' preferential-use gates G12 and G14 for $30.2 million during Spirit's restructuring. As Travel Weekly and Half as Interesting note, snapping up those Concourse G gates gave United extra room to support added flying while keeping rivals from capturing every available opening. Even when federal caps later trimmed peak-hour schedules from initial prepares, United's sheer departure base and hub connectivity kept it positioned as O'Hare's dominant carrier.

    For United, defending O'Hare also means holding off challengers on high-value domestic and international connecting flows until long-term terminal capacity comes online. The hope is that through pairing route expansion with targeted gate acquisitions and vocal executive messaging, United can accept and manage near-term scheduling friction rather than cede ground in its home city.

    Facing a gate redetermination that shifted space toward United ahead of the October 2025 handover, American Airlines took the fight to court in May 2025, accusing the city of mishandling the redistribution process under the airport's use-and-lease framework. As documented in federal and state court filings from Justia, American challenged the reallocation only to see its efforts to halt the transfer fall short in federal court and later in Cook County Chancery Court. Even with its Terminal 3 footprint squeezed, standing at 66 gates per Chicago Department of Aviation facility data as of April 1, 2026, following reallocation adjustments that varied across reporting snapshots, American pressed ahead with schedule additions rather than conceding relevance in Chicago.

    To claw back concourse space outside the city's annual formula, American, like United, moved swiftly in Spirit Airlines' bankruptcy proceedings to acquire two preferential-use gates, G8 and G10, on Concourse G for $30 million. Based on information from Culture Guru, it is clear how strategic that purchase was for American: gates G8 and G10 sit right next to an existing Admirals Club lounge, giving ground crews and connecting passengers closer proximity and easier operations. Adding those two gates helped offset part of American's redetermination loss while reinforcing its push to build up departures across domestic and regional markets.

    For American CEO Robert Isom, holding firm at O'Hare is a deliberate statement that American will not be pushed aside or treated as a secondary afterthought in Chicago. As Chicago Magazine highlights, Isom has framed O'Hare as a vital hub for local and connecting travelers while rolling out added flights to defend share. That combination of courtroom pushback, opportunistic gate buying, and schedule investment highlights American fighting to keep its Midwestern hub intact despite steep headwinds.

    Aggressive schedule padding collided directly with airfield construction constraints in spring 2026, prompting the Federal Aviation Administration to concern a scheduling limits order on April 20, 2026, capping daily operations at 2,708 flights between 6:00 AM and 11:59 PM Central Time, as per Forbes.

    After published peak schedules pushed past 3,038 to 3,080 daily operations, well beyond what taxiway rehabilitation, ramp work, and staffing could reliably handle, the agency intervened under Section 41722 to curb congestion and later extended the order through October 30, 2027. Enforcing half-hour limits ranging from 30 to 84 operations pushed carriers to trim excess frequencies, delay seasonal route starts, or upgauge aircraft rather than fly schedules that could not clear the ground cleanly.

    That federal ceiling exposes how tightly the gate fight is bound to O'Hare's buildout, where the ORDNext expansion has seen its price tag climb from an initial $8.5 billion estimate to $12 billion while major milestones stretch toward 2034 and 2035. Some pieces have moved ahead, including Terminal 5's 10-gate addition, Concourse L's three-gate expansion, and a $1.455 billion contract for the 19-gate Concourse D, but the wider Global Terminal is not slated to open until 2034, as reported by The Points Guy. With fresh gates arriving slowly and taxiway work narrowing surface margins, airlines cannot just build their way out of the issue in the near term.

    It has been revealed that instead, every incremental concourse opening or construction adjustment carries heightened stakes because overall capacity is constrained by active building zones and long taxi times. Multi-year phased delivery means carriers need to put schedule ambition against real-world ramp and runway throughput. In a constrained environment, regulatory flight caps and phased construction make every available gate a scarce asset.

    Co-branded credit cards and frequent-flyer loyalty ecosystems that generate billions of dollars in high-margin partner revenue for major US carriers have a lot to do with this story. As Half as Interesting explains, airlines rely on card issuers and loyalty partnerships for lucrative non-ticket cash flows that help underpin overall profitability. In a major metropolitan market like Chicago, home to deep corporate travel accounts and high-spending cardholders, winning local flyer preference means capturing everyday card spend and repeat mileage redemptions, not just filling seats.

    That loyalty dynamic helps explain why Chicago carries outsized strategic weight compared with markets where American previously lost ground. American ceded shares in Fresh York and Los Angeles and began to lean more on hubs in Philadelphia and Phoenix, leaving Chicago as a critical battleground if it wants to stay top-of-wallet among major-spending coastal and Midwestern flyers. Conversely, Travel Weekly highlights how hub scale and schedule breadth reinforce card acquisition, because travelers who cannot conveniently fly or connect on an airline tend to shift both their trips and their credit card spend elsewhere.

    Industry observers note that at the same time, executive debates over loyalty economics show just how fiercely both carriers guard their Chicago customer base. Even as United executives have pushed back against oversimplified narratives that airline profits come effortlessly from credit cards alone, pointing to the real operational cost of carrying award travelers, both United and American treat Chicago loyalty as too valuable to surrender lightly. In this light, concourse gates are the door to a much bigger prize: long-term brand security among Chicago's flyers.

    According to recent reports, what began as a dispute over departure-share gate formulas has become a test of endurance where courtroom rulings, federal scheduling caps, and loyalty economics converge at Chicago O'Hare. United and American are each fighting to protect a hub that anchors regional connectivity and high-value cardholder engagement, even as aggressive schedule padding runs headlong into physical runway and construction limits. Neither carrier can afford to treat O'Hare as expendable territory when hub scale directly shapes both flight reliability and long-term customer retention.

    The FAA scheduling limits extension runs through October 30, 2027; subsequent appellate and trial proceedings following the Illinois Appellate Court's November 19, order in American Airlines v. City of Chicago (Illinois Courts), and phased ORDNext milestones such as Concourse D, Concourse E, and the Global Terminal stretching into the 2030s are landmark turning points that are upcoming. How both airlines balance disciplined schedule growth against those regulatory and construction guardrails will decide once and for all who is at the helm of O'Hare's next era.

    #111302. Tech Report: Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (978 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop.
    • However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick.
    • Industry observers note that on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

    However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

    Industry observers note that on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

    It has been revealed that the plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then promptly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

    According to recent reports, after the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

    In a recent development, once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

    There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

    A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

    According to recent reports, what explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

    In other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

    Recent findings suggest that in this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

    However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

    So while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety issue. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

    A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

    Sources indicate that while this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety concern, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

    What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that an Alaska Airlines pilot reportedly walked away from his aircraft during boarding on Saturday morning after US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested two passengers on a Seattle jet bridge.
    • According to recent reports, the arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) as passengers boarded Alaska flight AS1306 to Los Angeles, which ended up being delayed by more than three hours.
    • According to recent reports, the incident occurred on Saturday morning as Alaska passengers were boarding a Boeing 737-800 bound for Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that an Alaska Airlines pilot reportedly walked away from his aircraft during boarding on Saturday morning after US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested two passengers on a Seattle jet bridge. Two flight attendants were also noted to be so overwhelmed by the incident that they asked to be replaced.

    According to recent reports, the arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) as passengers boarded Alaska flight AS1306 to Los Angeles, which ended up being delayed by more than three hours. Video footage of the incident, which has sparked widespread outrage, highlights masked officers struggling with travelers near the aircraft door.

    According to recent reports, the incident occurred on Saturday morning as Alaska passengers were boarding a Boeing 737-800 bound for Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). Speaking to local radio station KUOW, passenger Aidan Mendoza said masked ICE agents struggled with a man and a woman on the jet bridge at Gate N9, leaving around 50 passengers pressed against the jet bridge wall.

    Amid the chaos, Mendoza said an Alaska pilot walked back up the jet bridge looking uncomfortable and unsure of what to do, adding that "he didn't come back." KUOW also reports that two Alaska flight attendants were so overwhelmed that they asked to be "subbed out." Mendoza decided not to board the flight, saying a gate agent removed him from the passenger list before customer service refunded his ticket.

    In a statement to Simple Flying, an Alaska spokesperson did not confirm whether any crew members had to be replaced, but stated it was "not provided advance notice of the enforcement action" and is "working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred." The spokesperson added,.

    Recent findings suggest that "We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306. We recognize how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests.".

    In a statement, ICE remarked it had launched an operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza (who is unrelated to passenger Aidan Mendoza), a Mexican national who it said had overstayed his visa. The agency claimed other travelers "began to obstruct and assault" officers during the arrest, while a second passenger, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, "hurled hot coffee on the officers." ICE said Hernandez Mejia, also from Mexico, had overstayed her visa and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

    It has been revealed that the Port of Seattle, which operates the airport, said it was "outraged" by the incident, emphasizing that immigration enforcement at SEA takes place without its involvement or knowledge. According to the Port, local federal immigration authorities had previously agreed to protocols at the airport, and it is now investigating whether any of those agreements were breached.

    Saturday's arrests drew strong criticism from Washington officials, including Governor Bob Ferguson, who noted ICE was "completely and totally out of control." Ferguson added that he was looking into how the agents accessed the jet bridge and whether they violated a state law prohibiting law enforcement officers, including federal immigration agents, from wearing face coverings.

    ICE has stepped up arrests at US airports since the summer to apprehend travelers overstaying visas. Other notable cases include a woman from Ecuador escorted off a jet bridge in Denver in July, and a Southwest Airlines flight attendant taken into custody while on the job at Nashville International Airport (BNA).

    Airlines have little control over immigration enforcement at the gate. Airlines for America (A4A), which represents the largest US carriers, noted in August that it was holding discussions with ICE and TSA to ensure proper procedures were in place when law enforcement activity takes place at airports.

    Airline unions have been more outspoken, such as the Association of Professional Flight Attendants (APFA), which represents more than 26,000 American Airlines flight attendants. APFA recently noted it was "deeply alarmed" by ICE's escalating tactics and warned it could put passengers and crew in danger.
