    Why JSX Just Bought New Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired New Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.
    • If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.
    • Recent findings suggest that let’s start with a little context.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired New Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.

    If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.

    Recent findings suggest that let’s start with a little context. JSX is a public charter air carrier, which operates a fleet of nearly 60 planes, most of which are Embraer E135s and E145s.

    It has been revealed that it operates as a Part 135 operator, meaning it’s not technically an airline, as it’s using a loophole that allows it to not use standard TSA security screening, hire pilots with fewer than 1,500 hours, etc. Basically what’s happening is that one subsidiary sells the tickets, and then another subsidiary operates the flights, so it’s technically a “charter” (with 30 people who don’t know one another).

    Recent findings suggest that then there’s Upcoming Pacific Airlines, one of the strangest airline startups we’ve ever seen, and which I’ve covered extensively. The airline acquired some Boeing 757s, and the business proposal was to connect North America and Asia via Anchorage (ANC).

    In a recent development, the business model made zero sense in the first place, though there was some funding there, and they even invested in constructing a lounge in Anchorage, even though those flights never did happen. The airline did briefly fly from (ONT) to Nashville (BNA) — as one does — before ultimately going out of business.

    It has been revealed that that brings us to the news. New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with Embraer E145s that are leased from JSX, as reported by IshrionA. According to a Department of Transportation filing, the airline intends to resume flights with planes featuring 42 seats, which is higher than the 30-seat limit you’ll find on current JSX planes.

    JSX acquires Fresh Pacific Airlines.New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with ERJ 145 leased from JSX. pic.twitter.com/uMMS0J2fZy.

    On the surface, this of course makes absolutely no sense. Fresh Pacific Airlines was out of business, and the business model made no sense. So why would JSX buy an airline and then lease planes to it?

    Recent findings suggest that long story short, this seems to be a play to acquire a cheap Part 121 certificate. A Part 121 operator is a company that’s allowed to operate scheduled air transport… in other words, a “real” airline. As I mentioned above, JSX has historically been a Part 135 operator, and that explicitly means it’s not an airline. It’s a public charter air carrier, so it’s not a “real” airline.

    It has been revealed that going back a couple of years, we know that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was considering cracking down on carriers like JSX, since they definitely don’t operate within the spirit of the rules. That’s not to say that JSX did anything wrong, because by the letter of the law, they’re following it exactly. It’s just that the letter of the law makes no sense, and clearly doesn’t reflect the intent behind distinguishing between Part 121 and Part 135 operators.

    Under Trump, there was no scrutiny of this. However, with Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, I imagine JSX leaders may be worried that there could again be more scrutiny. If nothing else, buying a cheap Part 121 certificate is a good insurance policy, in case the government does crack down. After all, these can basically be “sold,” while acquiring one from scratch can be grueling process.

    Sources indicate that I wouldn’t assume that anything will really operate with Newly introduced Pacific Airlines branding, or based on a New Pacific Airlines business model. Instead, I imagine the idea is that JSX will start dabbling in Part 121 operations, which is why these planes will have more seats (above the 30-seat cap that’s allowed), since that’s no longer a factor.

    It has been revealed that if the government were to crack down on Part 135 operators, JSX could move to Part 121 operations. However, they’d have to make lots of changes, from their pilot hiring, to the way passengers are screened.

    JSX has just bought Fresh Pacific, the airline with an absurd business model that went bankrupt. No, JSX isn’t inspired by the concept of flying Boeing 757s to Asia. Instead, this is clearly the cheapest way for JSX to acquire a Part 121 certificate, which would be required for the carrier to continue operations in the event that the government were to crack down on the Part 135 operator loophole.

    It’s going to be interesting to see how this evolves, both since JSX seems to have looks to operate Part 121 operations in the near future, and also to see how JSX’s business model would evolve if the Part 135 concept were blocked.

    What do you make of this JSX Part 121 play?

    It has been revealed that the British first edition of The Managerial Revolution that I picked up in a Charing Cross Road shop a quarter century ago tells us much about the work itself. I’ve read it four times, conscripted it as an airplane companion, and brought it to the beach. Yet its binding remains strong, its cover quite flexible, and its pages yellowing but intact. We no longer much refer to let alone read such 1941 bestsellers as Clifton Fadiman’s Reading I’ve Liked or Margaret Leech’s Reveille in Washington. But James Burnham, much like my strong and solid copy of his most famous book, endures.

    It has been revealed that burnham, who entered the world 121 years ago Sunday and left it nearly 40 years ago, very much remains part of the Great Conversation. The Managerial Revolution, anticipating as it did the ascension of technocrats, specialists, and the bureaucratic elite as a sort of ruling class, surely helped in that regard. Burnham remains read, despite no Burnhamite clique in academia or organized faction among movement conservatives dedicated to advancing his ideas. Kirkians, Straussians, and Randians exist. Why no James Burnham Preservation Society with an accompanying secret handshake?

    In a recent development, daniel J. Flynn, the author of The Man Who Invented Conservatism: The Unlikely Life of Frank S. Meyer, is an American Spectator senior editor, visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution, and YouTuber @RightWingWilderness.

    On “The Complex Reputation of James Burnham”.

    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
    • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

    Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

    “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries stated, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

    According to recent reports, the proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

    Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Substantial Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

    Recent findings suggest that “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

    In a recent development, on healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for prepares purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

    When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    The Upcoming York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

    “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

    Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

    Industry observers note that without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

    Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

    This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

    • Manufactured from 1949 to 1964, the de Havilland DH.106 Comet was the world's first commercial jet airliner.
    • According to recent reports, the jet rose to enormous historical significance for the entire aviation industry and was also the high watermark for British commercial aviation.
    • According to recent reports, the idea for a British jet airliner was born during the Second World War.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Manufactured from 1949 to 1964, the de Havilland DH.106 Comet was the world's first commercial jet airliner. It was powered by four jet engines and included a pressurized cabin. The engines were built into the wing roots, giving it a distinct, aerodynamically sleek appearance.

    According to recent reports, the jet rose to enormous historical significance for the entire aviation industry and was also the high watermark for British commercial aviation. Yet the Comet's success was short-lived. Its design made it prone to metal fatigue after repeated pressurization. Two early fatal hull losses permanently damaged its market position.

    According to recent reports, the idea for a British jet airliner was born during the Second World War. The Brabazon Committee recommended developing and producing a pressurized, nonstop transatlantic mail aircraft that could carry a 2,200 lb (1,000 kg) payload. The conventional wisdom at the time was that jet engines were not fuel efficient or reliable enough for transatlantic flight. De Havilland head Sir Geoffrey de Havilland used his influence to propose that there should be a specification for a turbojet-powered design.

    The Brabazon Committee awarded a contract to de Havilland to produce its Type 106, initially considered a small, short-range jet aircraft, while other manufacturers were also commissioned for other designs. The Type 106 featured untested elements and was financially risky, but the British Overseas Airways Corporation (BOAC) placed an order for 10 aircraft.

    In a recent development, de Havilland put together a design team to create the aircraft, which was led by Ronald Bishop, the brain behind the Mosquito fighter-bomber. The initial concept was for an unconventional tailless design. However, BOAC's demand to increase capacity from 24 to 36 seats forced the designers to opt for something more conventional. The final version was named DH.106 Comet in December 1947. First orders were then completed, with both BOAC and British South American Airways invested. They committed to 14 aircraft, to be delivered by 1952.

    Industry observers note that the first Comet prototype was ready in 1949. On its maiden flight, the jet took off from Hatfield Aerodrome and flew for 31 minutes. John "Cats Eyes" Cunningham, a former RAF night-fighter pilot, was at the controls. The second prototype, G-ALZK, was registered in July 1950 and amassed 500 flying hours. Qantas sent its experts to observe its operations.

    According to recent reports, the first production aircraft was G-ALYP, nicknamed "Yoke Peter", which first flew on January 9, 1951. The jet completed the world's first jetliner flight with paying passengers. It flew from London to Johannesburg. By September 1952, all the aircraft in BOAC's initial order had arrived. G-ALYZ was the last to be delivered, carrying cargo on South American routes according to simulated passenger schedules. On August 4, 1952, Prince Philip returned from the Helsinki Olympic Games on the aircraft.

    The table below uses BAE Systems data to show the specifications for the Comet 1:.

    4 x De Havilland Ghost 50 engines producing 4,450 lbf each.

    1,300 nautical miles (2,400 km).

    Early Comet operations demonstrated its viability in commercial operations. It carried 30,000 passengers and was profitable on flights with a load factor as low as 43%. The jet also greatly outperformed its piston-engined rivals. The jet flew 55% faster, and its faster climb rate cut flight time.

    Popular Mechanics magazine wrote in 1952 that the Comet was between three and five years ahead of any other proposed jet aircraft. Writer Aubrey Cookman rode the aircraft on a mammoth six-stop trip from London to Johannesburg. "Scheduled eight-mile-a-minute travel in the stratosphere is here. I did it, and from now on so can you," Cookman begins. "Regular airline life insurance was available at the usual rate and I suspect a few snapped it up," they later admitted.

    The trip took 17 hours and 16 minutes, but was still about twice as fast as contemporary piston aircraft. These multi-stop odysseys were typical in the Comet's first years of operation. In the summer of 1953, eight Comets left London per week, with the destinations being Johannesburg, Tokyo, Singapore and Colombo. The Tokyo flight took 36 hours, with the same trip on BOAC's DC-4M-4 Argonaut taking over 86 hours.

    The table below shows the fleet sizes of the Comet's most significant operators in the 1960s, using data collected by Simple Flying:.

    From 1953, several other airlines placed orders for the Comet. Union Aéromaritime de Transport and Air France both ordered three Comet 1As, which had greater fuel capacity. De Havilland also developed the Comet 2, which had better engines and was longer. Air India, British Commonwealth Pacific Airlines, Japan Airlines and more made orders, although Qantas concluded that the Comet wasn't yet ready for its London to Canberra route.

    Industry observers note that across its service, the Comet was involved in 25 hull-loss accidents, 13 of which were fatal, leading to the tragic deaths of 492 people, according to Aviation Safety Network. That is 22% of all airframes built. The first accident came on October 26, 1952. BOAC Flight 115 was attempting to take off from Rome Ciampino G. B. Pastine Airport (CIA) when it failed to get airborne. It ran into rough ground at the end of the airport. Just two passengers suffered minor injuries, but the aircraft never flew again.

    A fresh Canadian Pacific Airlines Comet 1A suffered a similar accident in March 1953, resulting in the deaths of five crew and six passengers. It was the first fatal jetliner crash. The first airborne fatal jetliner crash occurred on May 2, 1953. BOAC Flight 783 crashed in a thunderstorm shortly after takeoff from Calcutta-Dum Dum Airport (CCU). The jet was seen hurtling towards the ground with no wings. All 43 people on board died.

    The following year saw the notorious Comet disasters of 1954. These were BOAC Flight 781 and South African Airways Flight 201. Flight 781 was the most deadly, with the aircraft breaking up in midair 20 minutes after takeoff from Ciampino.

    Industry observers note that "The cost of solving the Comet mystery must be reckoned neither in money nor in manpower," said British Prime Minister Winston Churchill. The Royal Aircraft Establishment at Farnborough led an investigation into the accidents. Its work showed that cabin pressurization cycles had caused metal fatigue cracks. The stress had been concentrated near windows and hatch corners, as well as around the automatic direction-finding (ADF) antenna cutout. These small areas of fatigue were sufficient to cause the thin-skinned fuselage to fail, leading the aircraft to break up in midair with deadly consequences.

    In a recent development, the findings resulted in the Comet 1 fleet being grounded in 1954. Future Comet iterations, like the Comet 4, had thicker skin, and areas prone to stress were also targeted. De Havilland completed a refit program to strengthen the skin and wing structure of existing aircraft and install rounder windows.

    The Comet 4 first flew in April 1958, marking the Comet's return to service. Comet 3 customers canceled their orders and switched to the newer iteration, which had improved fuel capacity. BOAC used the jet for regular services from London to New York, completing the trip in an incredibly short six hours and 12 minutes. It was the first jetliner to make a nonstop transatlantic trip. Yetat this time, the Boeing 707 was coming into service, as was the Douglas DC-8. These American aircraft were larger, faster, and had a better range. The days of Britain dominating jet aviation were numbered.

    Sources indicate that A Dan-Air Comet (pictured above) performed the final flight of the world's first commercial jet aircraft on November 9, 1980. The British carrier flew nearly 50 Comets, usually acquiring them secondhand during the 1960s and 1970s, with three Comet variants in the fleet. The final flight saw a Comet 4C take off from London Gatwick Airport (LGW). The plane then made a low pass at London Heathrow Airport (LHR) before making another low pass at RAF Brize Norton. The destination honored G-BDIW's former owner, the RAF, where it was registered as XR398.

    Industry observers note that the passengers received certificates showing they had been on the last flight. The jet then traveled on to Germany for preservation at the Flugausstellung Peter Junior museum in Hermeskeil. The service was not the last time that a Comet took to the skies. The UK Ministry of Technology continued to use the jet to research avionics, radar, and radio-based technology. That aircraft, XS235, continued these duties until its final retirement in March 1997. It concluded 45 years of the Comet being seen over skies in Britain and around the world. The plane is now part of the Cold War Jets Collection at Bruntingthorpe Aerodrome in Leicestershire.

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Qatar-Gifted 747 Air Force One Claims 2 Records On 15-Hour Nonstop Flight From China

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article was updated on Sunday, November 22, 2026, to include context on the record claims and the aircraft's outbound trip.
    • Sources indicate that the Qatari-gifted Boeing 747-8, now flying as the VC-25B Bridge aircraft, set two Air Force records on its return from Shenzhen, China, according to the White House.
    • According to recent reports, the aircraft left Shenzhen at 5:54 PM local time on November 19 and landed at Joint Base Andrews at 8:01 PM local time with no refueling stop, carrying President Donald Trump home from the APEC summit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article was updated on Sunday, November 22, 2026, to include context on the record claims and the aircraft's outbound trip. It was originally published on Saturday, November 21, 2026.

    Sources indicate that the Qatari-gifted Boeing 747-8, now flying as the VC-25B Bridge aircraft, set two Air Force records on its return from Shenzhen, China, according to the White House. The jet reportedly made the heaviest takeoff in Air Force history at just under one million pounds, and also flew the longest nonstop Air Force One flight to date, lasting nearly 15 hours.

    According to recent reports, the aircraft left Shenzhen at 5:54 PM local time on November 19 and landed at Joint Base Andrews at 8:01 PM local time with no refueling stop, carrying President Donald Trump home from the APEC summit. The jet cruised at 33,000 feet and averaged 500 knots (926 km/h), passing over Shanghai, Tokyo, Shemya, Winnipeg, and Cleveland. Trump put the duration at about 14.5 hours and said the trip normally takes closer to 20 with a fuel stop, which he credited to newer equipment.

    The 747-8i on which the VC-25B is based has a maximum takeoff weight of 987,000 pounds (447,694 kg), which TWZ notes exceeds that of a fully loaded C-5M Galaxy, and an endurance of 15 to 16 hours is commonly quoted for the type. The 7,500 nautical miles (13,890 km) flown sits inside the nearly 7,800 nautical miles (14,446 km) Boeing lists for a commercial 747-8i.

    That comparison has limits. The Bridge jet is probably much lighter than a fully loaded airliner even with maximum fuel, although extra tanks may have been added during conversion, so its true maximum range remains unclear. The records therefore show the airframe operating near the upper edge of its envelope, not beyond what the type was designed to do.

    According to a card handed to the accompanying press pool:.

    "The VC-25B conducted the heaviest takeoff in Air Force history, at just under one million pounds, and completed the longest nonstop Air Force One sortie to date, at nearly 15 hours.".

    The Bridge jet cannot be refueled in flight, and neither can the two purpose-built VC-25Bs that Boeing is under contract to deliver. TWZ reports that the requirement was dropped in 2017 as a cost-cutting measure, and that the upcoming E-4C command post aircraft, built on the same 747 model, will keep the capability. The two aging VC-25As can take on fuel in the air, though only in emergencies, and they stopped in Alaska to refuel on the way home from this trip.

    Range requirements add to the concern. The original VC-25B requirement was roughly 7,100 nautical miles (13,149 km), later revised to 5,900 (10,927 km), while the Air Force fact sheet lists about 6,800 (12,594 km) for the VC-25A. TWZ concludes that unless the new jets exceed the revised figure by a wide margin, they cannot fly this route nonstop, and it points to the weight of nuclear hardening, defenses, and tailored systems as the likely cause.

    Simple Flying puts the cost of the VC-25B program at $5.3 billion, driven by protection against electromagnetic pulses, missile evasion, and secure global communications. TWZ adds that time aloft is central to continuity of government planning.

    The White House remains the only source for the two flight records so far. As it stands, the claims came from the card handed to the press pool, Trump's own remarks, along with a post on X by White House communications director Steven Cheung. Neither the Air Force nor Boeing has publicly confirmed either figure, and TWZ reports that it has contacted both for confirmation.

    The nonstop flight home was also a contrast to the earlier outbound trip to Asia. On November 16, the Bridge jet stopped in Alaska to refuel on its way to Manila, landing at Fairbanks International Airport instead of its planned stop in Anchorage. The White House blamed freezing rain around Anchorage and dismissed reports about the diversion as "fear-mongering slop.".

    The mission also brought all three presidential 747s to Asia. The Bridge jet, painted in the red, white, and blue livery Trump has favored, carried the president, while the older VC-25As, registered 82-8000 and 92-9000, accompanied it, and all three were seen together in Manila. A second aircraft routinely travels as a mechanical backup, but it is not known whether the third jet continued to China.

    The Bridge aircraft arrived at Joint Base Andrews on June 19, intended to serve until the long-term VC-25B is delivered. It debuted as Air Force One on July 1, flying the president to North Dakota, and the Air Force accepted it less than two months before that. L3Harris completed the conversion in 10 months, and TWZ indicates significant questions remain about whether the jet can support the full range of mission requirements, though officials and the contractor say concerns have been addressed.

    The final modification cost is undisclosed, with an earlier estimate of under $400 million. Analysts had speculated that the interim jet was unsuited to international missions because of its limited modifications, a view the recent China trip undercuts. The VC-25Bs are expected in 2028, and the VC-25As are scheduled to retire in 2029.

    #111286. The American Genius of Madden

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (867 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    The American Genius of Madden

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that hang on at the start of David O.
    • Industry observers note that the key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football.
    • Madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that hang on at the start of David O. Russell’s Madden, as its story of the Oakland Raiders football coach John Madden shifts between semidocumentary and biopic. Russell’s uneven, sketchy narrative steadily turns into a probing human comedy. It’s also a slyly monumental tale of American genius found in an Everyman’s commonplace ambition.

    Industry observers note that the key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football. Cage enters the mindset of a sports fanatic who is also an artist, devising plays and strategies that, considering his size and vision, earn him the nickname “Buddha.” But this is not one of those freak-outs that Cage is known for; he seems to transform himself into John Candy — broad-beamed with a tuft of blond hair and a convincing smile. Cage commits to this genial eccentric who, despite his unreachable idiosyncrasy, is harmless, lovable yet tough — an authentic, original American.

    Madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend. This thick-and-thin Laurel-and-Hardy pair sustain an unlikely partnership. It’s one of the most remarkable depictions of brotherhood in movies — a friendship that persists over temperamental tensions, even after Madden leaves the team and pursues media entrepreneurship to sustain his love of the sport. Madden the broadcaster converts his playbook ingenuity and follows his father’s advice: “Get away with doing what you love for as long as you possibly can.”.

    Russell redeems himself with the oddest-yet-normal collection of American eccentrics. Acting on the edge of parody, Cage and Bale, with their uncanny sincerity, reward Russell’s interest in quirkiness. (Madden hears Davis’s voice in his head.) The fascinating scoundrels of Russell’s terrific American Hustle were preoccupied with manipulating one another. Here, friendship, comradeship, teamwork, and family complications are genuinely recognizable. Scenes that emulate a documentary approach — Madden’s wife Virginia (gung ho comedienne Kathryn Hahn) rivals Jennifer Lawrence’s volatility when speaking directly to the camera — satirize realism to fulfill the non-cynical view of national character that Russell fumbled in the bohemian sojourn of Amsterdam. No wonder De Niro is left out of this particular silver-lined playbook.

    Nicolas Cage (John Madden) in Madden.

    Chuck Zlotnick/Amazon MGM Studios.

    The patchwork of styles in Madden suggests that Russell investigates American eccentricity as he goes along, finding his way back to the coast-to-coast realness that made his Flirting with Disaster so exhilarating (as in Madden’s surreal, unapologetic pitch for the unique holiday dish the Turducken). Russell adopts Madden’s football-analysis style, such as on-screen telestrator vectors, to humorously examine Madden’s own career shifts and twists of personality (Madden instructing his players, or meeting colleagues Pat Summerall, Howard Cosell, and Bob Costas).

    Recent findings suggest that A dull-witted filmmaker, say James Cameron, would choose an “immersive” style for a movie concerned with the gestalt of football. But Russell’s film is also about the phenomenon of a sport that becomes a vanguard of technology and culture. Madden is pursued by Trip Hawkins (John Mulaney), founder of video game company EA (Electronic Arts), who wants to translate Madden’s football theories for a fresh generation of at-home fans and gamers. Hawkins’s proposal is scored to Beethoven’s Ninth — another example of Russell’s wit, matching the film’s eclectic score from Barry White and Talking Heads to N.W.A. (“You don’t want to know what that means,” Davis says to Madden.).

    Through Madden and Hawkins’s acumen, Russell treats the discovery of a fresh world as an aftereffect of folk intelligence and ingenuity. Genius is kidded when Hawkins’s team of four-eyed computer nerds demonstrate jock potential after applying Madden’s plays to their algorithms. It’s a sweet way of conveying the phenomenon that would turn EA’s Madden NFL video game franchise into a $4 billion enterprise (some estimates raise that into double digits), with annual compensation going to the Madden family estate.

    More notable, Russell (who co-wrote the script with Cambron Clark) sees Madden as a visionary who proudly summarizes TV sportscasting as “They state the obvious, which is f***ing boring.” My only complaint is that Robert Richardson’s photography tends toward frowzy (perhaps deliberately aping TV docs), not as splendid as Oliver Stone’s Any Given Sunday — the greatest football movie ever made.

    Madden itself shares biopic sensibility with John Ford’s The Wings of Eagles, respectfully eschewing its subject’s mortality for an optimistic appreciation of a man’s potential. It is unique to American character and the experience of competition and dreams of the NFL Hall of Fame that Madden shared with Al Davis. Russell’s tribute comes complete with a motto: “You make people feel good and alive and good to be American, and I’m not standing in the way of that.” Thus Russell proves his own resilience and the achievement of a new folkloric genre struggling to emerge.

    Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of Newly introduced Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

    On “The American Genius of Madden”.

    Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Industry observers note that hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    Sources indicate that that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an key part of it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” stated Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley mentioned that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very firm that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    “We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a manufacturer’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She noted Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also remarked that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    Sources indicate that “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles mentioned. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    If you’re looking for a simple card that earns a solid return at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers, this one is worth a look. It has no annual fee (Rates & Fees), a decent welcome bonus, a great intro APR offer, and some useful bonus categories that cover a good chunk of everyday spending.

    This post is my in-depth Blue Cash Everyday Card review, so I’ll cover the bonus categories, the credits and perks, and how this card compares to both the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express and the Citi Double Cash® Card.

    Review: Learn more about the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express.

    First, here’s an overview of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday benefits and value proposition, from fees, to rewards, to the welcome bonus:.

    I also put together my list of pros and cons for the Blue Cash Everyday Card:.

    Sources indicate that when applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, eligibility rules, and fees, are major considerations. So below I’ll cover the details of that for the Amex Blue Cash Everyday.

    Industry observers note that the Amex Blue Cash Everyday is offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s a reasonable bonus for a no annual fee card, and the spending requirement is low enough that most people should be able to hit it. However, it’s also not that much to get excited about, compared to some of the other welcome offers out there.

    In a recent development, amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. Here are the main rules to be aware of:.

    Recent findings suggest that amex also has a pre-application eligibility tool that lets you check whether you’ll be approved for the card without any impact on your credit score. This is worth using if you’re not sure that you’ll qualify.

    The Blue Cash Everyday Card has no annual fee. Not the first year, not ever. That alone makes it worth considering as a long-term card in your wallet, even if it’s not your primary spender.

    Holding no annual fee cards long term is also a great way to help your credit score. About 30% of your score comes from credit utilization (the more available credit you have but don’t use, the better), and 15% comes from credit history length (the older your average account age, the better). A no annual fee card you keep open for years helps on both fronts.

    It has been revealed that the Blue Cash Everyday Card does have foreign transaction fees (2.7%) (Rates & Fees), so I wouldn’t use it for purchases in foreign currencies. Stick to domestic spending with this one, and find a card with no foreign transaction fees if you’ll be spending time abroad.

    The Amex Blue Cash Everyday has three main bonus categories, each earning 3% cash back on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%).

    Recent findings suggest that with the Blue Cash Everyday, you earn 3% back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). Earning 3% back at supermarkets with no annual fee is a solid deal, and this is one of the better no annual fee cards for U.S. supermarket spending.

    As with most grocery bonus categories, this generally won’t include warehouse clubs (like Costco), superstores (like Walmart or Target), convenience stores, or discount stores. Traditional supermarkets and grocery chains are what you’re looking for.

    With the Blue Cash Everyday, you also earn 3% back at U.S. gas stations on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This is one of the better no annual fee cards for gas station spending.

    It has been revealed that this is the bonus category that makes the Blue Cash Everyday stand out from its siblings. You earn 3% back on U.S. online retail purchases on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This covers purchases made on a website or app from a U.S. retail merchant that sells physical goods directly to consumers.

    In a recent development, given how much shopping happens online these days, this can be a really valuable category. You won’t find this bonus on many other cards.

    Industry observers note that for purchases outside the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is where the card falls short. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll definitely want to pair this with a card that offers a better return on everyday purchases.

    With the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits at a rate of 1.0 cents per point, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem.

    It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

    Benefits and credits can certainly help with justifying holding onto credit cards. In the case of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you wouldn’t expect very valuable perks, given the card’s lack of an annual fee. However, it’s an area where I’d say the card actually exceeds expectations, and offers solid value.

    According to recent reports, the Blue Cash Everyday offers up to $7 back per month (up to $84 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled Blue Cash Everyday to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscriptions are subject to auto-renewal. If you already pay for any of those services, this is an easy credit to use. (Enrollment required).

If you use Home Chef, this is a significant benefit. If you don’t, it’s probably not worth signing up just for the credit. (Enrollment required).

    Recent findings suggest that the Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 15 months from the date of account opening. After that, the variable APR is at the moment between 19.74% - 28.74% (Rates & Fees).

    It has been revealed that I generally recommend avoiding financing purchases through credit cards. But if a short-term 0% APR opportunity can help you manage a large purchase and you can pay it off before the rate increases, it’s a nice option to have.

    Another card benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

    Industry observers note that every Amex card gives you access to the Amex Offers program, which provides targeted deals with a variety of retailers. Different cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards means more chances to save.

    I try to have as many Amex cards as possible specifically to take advantage of this. Having a no annual fee card like this is ideal, since the card isn’t costing you anything, but you’re still getting access to potentially valuable offers.

    The Amex Blue Cash Everyday comes with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

    Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

    The Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers purchase protection of up to $1,000 per covered purchase for up to 90 days from the purchase date. You need to pay with the card in order to take advantage of this coverage.

    The Amex Blue Cash Everyday Card is a solid no annual fee cash back card with useful bonus categories at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers. The 3% rate in those categories is strong for a no annual fee card, and the Disney streaming credits, Home Chef credits, and Amex Offers add extra value on top.

    While there are several reasons to consider the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there are also a couple of alternatives that I think are better for most people.

    If you generally like the idea of the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there might still be a better play here. The Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express (learn more) is the premium version of the card, and it could be worth applying for it instead (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

    In a recent development, the massive question is whether the Preferred’s $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. annual fee (Rates & Fees) is worth the upgrade. If you spend at least $267 per month at U.S. supermarkets, the extra 3% (the Preferred earns 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases, then 1%) on groceries alone will cover the fee. The Preferred also adds 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming and 3% on transit, which the Everyday doesn’t offer.

    On the flip side, the Everyday has two things the Preferred doesn’t: 3% on U.S. online retail purchases and a 0% intro APR offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and not as much grocery shopping, the Everyday could be the better card.

    According to recent reports, one nice thing is that you could start with the Blue Cash Preferred (with a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95.), and if the math doesn’t work out, downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after year one. That way you get the bigger welcome bonus and can test the higher earning rates.

    While there are lots to like about the Blue Cash Everyday, it’s also not particularly well-rounded if you’re looking for an all-in-one cash back credit card.

    According to recent reports, the card offers 3% cash back at U.S. supermarkets, U.S. gas stations, and U.S. online retail purchases (up to certain limits), but on other purchases you’ll earn 1% cash back.

    According to recent reports, everyone will have to crunch the numbers for themselves, but 1% cash back is pretty uncompetitive nowadays for savvy consumers. For example, the no annual fee Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

    Industry observers note that the Blue Cash Everyday wins in its bonus categories, earning 3% at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers compared to the Double Cash’s flat 2%. But the Double Cash wins everywhere else, earning 2% on all purchases versus just 1%.

    According to recent reports, if your spending is heavily concentrated in supermarkets, gas, and online shopping, the Blue Cash Everyday will earn you more. If your spending is more spread out across lots of different categories, the Double Cash’s flat 2% on everything will likely come out ahead.

    The Double Cash also has a major advantage in flexibility. Its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners (in conjunction with a premium Citi card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card), giving those points the potential to be worth well more than 2 cents each. The Blue Cash Everyday’s rewards are purely cash back.

    It has been revealed that the ideal setup? Have both. Use the Blue Cash Everyday for supermarkets, gas, and online retail where it earns 3%, and the Double Cash for everything else at 2%.

    Sources indicate that I think the Blue Cash Everyday is a very decent cash back card with bonus categories most spenders can take advantage of. The card’s main weakness is the 1% rate on everything outside the bonus categories — and even on those categories once you reach the annual cap. For that reason, I’d recommend pairing it with a flat-rate card like the Citi Double Cash (2% on everything) to fill in the gaps. Together, they make a simple, effective, no annual fee credit card cash back setup.

    If you find yourself spending more at supermarkets over time, you can always upgrade to the Blue Cash Preferred for that 6% supermarket rate. But for a no annual fee, low-maintenance starting point, the Blue Cash Everyday is a great choice.

    LATAM Airlines unveils fresh A321XLR cabins with eye on US expansion

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The next frontier for the Airbus A321XLR is South America.
    • After opening dozens of upcoming transatlantic routes, the long-range narrow-body will make its debut with LATAM Airlines in March 2027.
    • LATAM, a close partner of Delta Air Lines, will outfit its fleet of XLRs with 174 seats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The next frontier for the Airbus A321XLR is South America.

    After opening dozens of upcoming transatlantic routes, the long-range narrow-body will make its debut with LATAM Airlines in March 2027. The airline has yet to say which routes the XLRs will fly, but executives have previously outlined opportunities to connect the U.S. and South America.

    LATAM, a close partner of Delta Air Lines, will outfit its fleet of XLRs with 174 seats. Business class will feature 12 lie-flat suites supplied by Thompson Aero Seating in a 1-1 layout with privacy doors.

    The suites include 19-inch personal entertainment screens, Bluetooth connectivity and in-seat charging options.

    Economy features 13-inch screens at each of the 126 seats, which are supplied by Recaro, plus Bluetooth connectivity and USB-C outlets. The cabin includes 36 extra-legroom seats.

    In a recent development, “The Airbus A321XLR allows us to take our value proposition to the next level and elevate the travel experience for our passengers,” remarked Paulo Miranda, the chief customer officer of LATAM, in a statement. He described the interior, which features red, orange and blue hues, as “inspired by South America.”.

    LATAM executives have mentioned it could fly the XLR on routes into the U.S. from its hub at Jorge Chavez International Airport (LIM) in Lima. However, those aims were called into question in May over the addition of a "connection fee" at LIM.

    According to recent reports, the airline and Delta serve six U.S. destinations from LIM: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Orlando International Airport (MCO) and, since January 2026, Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

    LATAM did not comment on specific route prepares for the XLR.

    The XLR is the second latest airplane type for LATAM in as many years. The airline took delivery of its first Embraer E195-E2 in October. It will use the small jet to expand its feeder network in Brazil and support additional long-haul, intercontinental flying.

    #111282. 5 Reasons A Passenger Can End Up On The US No-Fly List

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1479 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    5 Reasons A Passenger Can End Up On The US No-Fly List

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1479 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Air travel is one of the safest ways to travel, with airlines, airports, and government agencies working together to identify potential security threats before passengers board an aircraft.
    • Being placed on the No-Fly List is not simply a matter of attracting attention at an airport or having a disagreement with an airline.
    • In a recent development, one of the most straightforward reasons an individual can be placed on the US No-Fly List is posing a suspected threat to an aircraft or aviation security.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Air travel is one of the safest ways to travel, with airlines, airports, and government agencies working together to identify potential security threats before passengers board an aircraft. In the US, an notable part of this process is the federal No-Fly List, a government database designed to prevent individuals considered serious terrorism-related threats from accessing commercial aviation. Although the list is often associated with suspected terrorists, its inclusion criteria are more specific than many travelers realize.

    Being placed on the No-Fly List is not simply a matter of attracting attention at an airport or having a disagreement with an airline. An individual must first meet the reasonable suspicion standard for inclusion on the broader terrorist watchlist and then satisfy at least one additional criterion relating to terrorism and national security. From threats against aircraft to concerns about domestic terrorism, several circumstances can result in a passenger being prohibited from flying.

    In a recent development, one of the most straightforward reasons an individual can be placed on the US No-Fly List is posing a suspected threat to an aircraft or aviation security. The list's primary purpose is to prevent individuals who may carry out terrorist activities from accessing commercial flights, making threats against civil aviation particularly significant. This includes concerns about someone intending to hijack an aircraft, carry out an attack during a flight, or otherwise compromise passenger and crew safety.

    Sources indicate that the government considers threats against aviation particularly serious because of the potential consequences for everyone onboard. A commercial aircraft, whether it is a Boeing 737 operated by Southwest Airlines or an Airbus A350 operated by Delta Air Lines, carries hundreds of people who depend on security procedures for their protection. An individual reasonably suspected of planning a terrorist attack involving an aircraft could therefore meet the additional criteria required for No-Fly List designation.

    In a recent development, however, the existence of a threat does not necessarily mean someone must have attempted to board an aircraft with a weapon or previously carried out an attack. The government can consider information suggesting that an individual intends to participate in terrorist activity, including conduct undertaken in preparation for an attack. This is why intelligence gathering and information sharing between federal agencies play such an key role in aviation security.

    Importantly, an individual must also meet the underlying reasonable suspicion standard to be included on the terrorist watchlist. A passenger making an isolated, inappropriate comment at an airport would not automatically qualify for the No-Fly List. Authorities must consider whether available information establishes the required connection to terrorism and whether the additional aviation-related threat criterion is satisfied.

    Another reason a passenger may end up on the No-Fly List is suspected involvement in domestic terrorism. Unlike international terrorism, which involves activities connected to foreign organizations or overseas interests, domestic terrorism concerns terrorist activities directed at targets within the US. The government considers this a significant national security concern, particularly when intelligence suggests that an individual may be planning or preparing a violent attack.

    Sources indicate that domestic terrorism can involve threats against public buildings, government facilities, infrastructure, or groups of people within the country. An individual suspected of participating in preparations for such an attack may attract attention from federal authorities, particularly when evidence suggests an intention to use violence to achieve political, ideological, or other objectives. Where the reasonable suspicion standard and additional No-Fly List criteria are met, the individual can be prevented from boarding commercial aircraft.

    It has been revealed that the aviation connection is not always immediately obvious. Someone suspected of planning an attack on a location far away from an airport may still represent a concern to national security officials. Restricting access to commercial aviation can reduce the ability of a suspected terrorist to travel rapidly, reach potential targets, or move between locations while authorities assess available intelligence. The restrictions are therefore not limited to people suspected of attacking aircraft themselves.

    This distinction matters because the No-Fly List also addresses broader threats to the homeland. Someone suspected of planning domestic terrorist violence could qualify even if there is no specific allegation that they intend to hijack a flight or attack an airport. The government must still establish the relevant legal threshold rather than relying solely on an individual's political opinions, beliefs, or lawful activities.

    The third reason concerns individuals suspected of threatening US government facilities located outside the country. American embassies, consulates, and other government installations overseas can face security threats from terrorist organizations and individuals operating internationally. Protecting these locations and the personnel working inside them is an important part of US national security policy, and suspected terrorist activity directed against them can affect an individual's ability to travel.

    A person suspected of planning an attack against a US diplomatic facility abroad may satisfy one of the additional criteria for inclusion on the No-Fly List. Such facilities represent US diplomatic and government interests in countries where security conditions can be complicated. An attack could endanger government employees, local staff, visitors, and members of the public, while creating wider diplomatic and international security consequences.

    The concern does not necessarily involve an individual physically traveling to an overseas location to carry out an attack. Intelligence indicating that someone is helping organize, support, or prepare for terrorist activities can be relevant to the broader watchlisting process. Authorities may consider information gathered by intelligence agencies, law enforcement organizations, and other government partners when determining whether an individual meets the applicable requirements.

    Recent findings suggest that for airlines, the consequences of a designation can be significant. A passenger placed on the No-Fly List cannot simply choose another carrier to complete their journey through US airspace. The restriction applies to flights arriving in, departing from, or operating over US airspace, rather than being limited to a particular airline. Consequently, changing from an aircraft operated by United Airlines to one operated by American Airlines, for example, would not solve the restriction. The designation concerns the passenger, not the airline.

    A fourth reason involves an individual suspected of intending to carry out a violent terrorist act while also possessing the operational capability to do so. This criterion considers both the seriousness of an individual's suspected intentions and whether they have the practical ability to act on them. The government is not simply assessing whether someone has expressed extremist views; it is considering whether the person represents a credible potential threat.

    Operational capability can involve different circumstances depending on the information available to investigators. For example, authorities may consider an individual's connections, resources, access to support, and apparent involvement in preparations for terrorist activity. These factors can help establish whether a suspected threat is more than an expression of intent and whether the individual could realistically participate in a violent attack.

    In a recent development, this criterion also demonstrates why the reasonable suspicion standard is only one part of the No-Fly List framework. Someone may be reasonably suspected of having connections to terrorism and qualify for the broader terrorist watchlist without necessarily meeting the additional requirements for the No-Fly List. The government must establish further threat-related criteria before applying the aviation ban.

    Sources indicate that although the four preceding reasons describe the formal threat-related criteria, another key issue can affect passengers: mistaken identity or an outdated watchlist designation. Not every traveler who experiences problems boarding an aircraft is actually on the No-Fly List. Sometimes, a passenger shares a name or other identifying information with someone in a government security database, resulting in additional screening or travel complications.

    Recent findings suggest that the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) highlighted this matter in its 2025 report, Terrorist Watchlist: Nomination and Redress Processes for US Persons. The report explained that individuals can be incorrectly identified as someone on the watchlist or remain listed when their inclusion is no longer warranted. This can create difficulties when printing boarding passes, completing airport security procedures, or traveling internationally. Importantly, additional screening does not automatically mean someone has been placed on the No-Fly List.

    The scale of the wider watchlisting system also helps explain why identification problems matter. The terrorist watchlist contained more than one million names in 2024, although this figure covered the broader database rather than the No-Fly List alone. The GAO also examined approximately 20,000 redress inquiries submitted between December 2021 and September 2023. Only 1.5% were related to the terrorist watchlist, with many other complaints involving passengers selected for additional screening through other security procedures.

    Industry observers note that passengers who believe they have been incorrectly identified can seek assistance through the Department of Homeland Security Traveler Redress Inquiry Program. This process allows affected travelers to request a review of their circumstances and seek correction of identification problems. While these requests do not guarantee removal, they provide an established route for challenging an apparent error or a designation that may no longer be justified.

    Tech Report: Lufthansa Management Threatens To Massively Shrink Airline, Lay Off Employees

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization.
    • Unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great.
    • In a recent development, how is that working out?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization. 2026 was supposed to be an exciting turnaround year for Lufthansa, as it’s even the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

    Unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great. Earlier this year, the carrier dealt with massive labor issues, and back-to-back-to-back strikes. Just a few months ago, the organization’s senior management claimed it wanted to turn over a latest leaf with labor relations, and stop fighting with employees, so that it could find long term solutions.

    In a recent development, how is that working out? Well, Lufthansa pilots are just days from possibly being able to strike again, no agreement has been reached for long term peace with employees, and management is threatening to massively shrink its mainline operation. In other words, it’s just another day at Lufthansa!

    Sources indicate that lufthansa and its pilots have been in negotiations for quite some time over the future of the company. As you’d expect, broadly speaking, negotiations revolve around pay and future flying opportunities. As you’d expect at any airline, employees want as much flying as possible, and as big of a fleet as possible, since that’s what maximizes their compensation.

    Sources indicate that the problem with Lufthansa Group management is that the company’s solution to everything is to simply create fresh, low cost subsidiaries. And if Lufthansa Group management doesn’t like the terms with its subsidiaries, then it just shuts down the subsidiaries and creates new ones.

    Sources indicate that so that brings us to the current issue. Essentially, Lufthansa’s problem is that the airline doesn’t make money on short haul flights, given high costs and intense competition. So we’ve seen the carrier increasingly outsourcing this flying to Lufthansa City Airlines, a subsidiary with lower operating costs, operating the same kinds of planes as you’ll see in the mainline fleet.

    Lufthansa is asking its pilots to accept wage freezes, and is promising a certain level of career development opportunities. Pilots aren’t happy with what’s being proposed, so what’s Lufthansa’s solution?

    Management is reportedly proposing a fresh initiative to the supervisory board, which would see the core Lufthansa brand massively reduce its regional flying, and largely outsource this to lower cost operations, like Lufthansa City Airlines. The idea would be to make Lufthansa primarily a long haul airline, and then have much of the short haul flying be operated by a subsidiary.

    Lufthansa’s mainline fleet presently consists of 260+ planes, with another 120+ planes on order. One proposal would see the mainline fleet reduced to 100 long haul aircraft and 100 short haul aircraft, with other planes being assigned to Lufthansa City Airlines.

    One radical proposal could even see Lufthansa exclusively have a long haul fleet and ditch short haul flying, though it’s noted that this isn’t the most likely scenario, and it could take several years for something like that to be implemented.

    Sources indicate that keep in mind that going back to 2017, Lufthansa had guaranteed pilots a minimum fleet size of 325 aircraft, but it terminated that agreement at the end of 2021. So it’s really hard for employees to trust any promises by management, when they can just be terminated.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s no denying that labor relations can be incredibly challenging, and that the economics of intra-Europe flying are also tough, when you have competitors like Ryanair, though Lufthansa doesn’t face nearly as much competition on that front as other carriers. Then again, Frankfurt (FRA) and Munich (MUC) aren’t exactly massively leisure destinations either.

    Sources indicate that most airline employees want their organization to succeed, and just want to be compensated fairly. Admittedly economics don’t always align. But what I find incredibly toxic is the approach taken by Lufthansa management. Let’s compare it to a marriage (which I think is a fair way to view the relationship between management and employees, since they’re “stuck” with one another).

    Lufthansa’s approach is to constantly threaten employees by saying that “if you don’t do what we want, we’ll just get rid of you.” That’s simply not a good faith way to approach things. Why would Lufthansa employees trust management, when they’ve repeatedly torn up contracts, and shown employees they simply don’t care? It would be like threatening to leave your spouse every time you have an issue, rather than trying to find a solution.

    Industry observers note that nothing against Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr personally, but I don’t understand how the board thinks he’s the best person for the job. Where’s the accountability for the endless management mistakes that have horribly impacted Lufthansa’s bottom line? Lufthansa’s employees are paying the price for the lack of success that comes as a result of all of Lufthansa’s errors, from the botched Allegris rollout, to Lufthansa’s very bad luck with new aircraft orders.

    It has been revealed that and before anyone says “oh, but the unions,” contrast what has happened at Lufthansa Group to what has happened at Air France-KLM, under the leadership of Ben Smith. Smith has now been CEO at Air France for over eight years, and there hasn’t been a single strike under his leadership. Under the previous Air France-KLM CEO, there were endless strikes, and the situation got so bad that senior executives were being chased up a fence and having their clothes ripped off.

    It has been revealed that this reveals that good labor relations absolutely can happen, balancing the needs of employees and the manufacturer. But it requires showing employees that you actually care about the company and their future. What was one of Smith’s first orders of business when he took the job at Air France-KLM? He eliminated Joon, the low cost carrier at the airline that was supposed to basically be a labor arbitrage opportunity. That was a way to show employees how much he respected them, and that he wanted a fair agreement, rather than one that would undermine them.

    Meanwhile Spohr’s solution to literally everything is to just threaten to start upcoming subsidiaries or shut down existing subsidiaries. The irony is that Spohr started his career as a pilot, so you’d think he’d have respect for employees, having been on the other side. But clearly once he became senior management, his love for aviation turned into disdain for employees.

    A few months ago, Lufthansa management claimed it wanted to turn over a latest leaf when it comes to labor relations. That didn’t last long, because now the airline is back to its “do what we say or we’ll create a new subsidiary” approach.

    I don’t have a strong opinion on the exact negotiations as such. Obviously it’s a tough time for aviation, and intra-Europe flying is challenging. But if you ask me, the toxicity that has been created by Lufthansa management due to the lack of good faith negotiations just can’t be undone.

    If your only solution to everything is “oh, we’ll create a fresh subsidiary,” and if that doesn’t work, maybe it’s time for a new strategy. The fact that American CEO Robert Isom and Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr still have their jobs are two of the industry’s greatest mysteries.

    On Personalized Pricing, the FTC Got Ahead of the Evidence

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Americans should expect their federal agencies to be staffed by experts who gather evidence meticulously before proposing regulations disinterestedly.
    • Last month, the FTC ordered nine major companies — Delta Air Lines, Uber, and Instacart among them — “to provide detailed information that will allow the agency to study the use of personal data to set prices and compensation.” The agency, however, seems to have reached its conclusions already, given the contents of both its order and an enforcement policy proposed in August, which appears partial against personalized pricing and the businesses that employ it.
    • Vladlena Klymova is a policy analyst at the Taxpayers Protection Alliance.

    Americans should expect their federal agencies to be staffed by experts who gather evidence meticulously before proposing regulations disinterestedly. But that’s not what the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has done when it comes to personalized pricing.

    Last month, the FTC ordered nine major companies — Delta Air Lines, Uber, and Instacart among them — “to provide detailed information that will allow the agency to study the use of personal data to set prices and compensation.” The agency, however, seems to have reached its conclusions already, given the contents of both its order and an enforcement policy proposed in August, which appears partial against personalized pricing and the businesses that employ it.

    Vladlena Klymova is a policy analyst at the Taxpayers Protection Alliance.

    On “On Personalized Pricing, the FTC Got Ahead of the Evidence”.

    The Bilt Palladium Card is one of my favorite credit cards, and it’s the card that gets the most of my spending. Just to cover some of the very basics, the card has a $495 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers the following value proposition at the moment:.

In other words, this card earns me 3x points on up to $25,000 of spending per year, plus I’m being rewarded on my housing spending.

    #111277. Breaking: Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1007 w)
