    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., noted, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, stated Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization blueprint so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    According to recent reports, senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz noted that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., noted after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    According to recent reports, for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., stated the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    Sources indicate that “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott mentioned, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he remarked. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    According to recent reports, he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy stated, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he noted that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    It has been revealed that bedford stated he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    Sources indicate that the may be the entry-level card option for Atmos Rewards, but it's anything but basic. This card packs a punch with a free checked bag and preferred boarding on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flights, with a fan-favorite $99 Companion Fare for cardholders who meet the spending requirements.

    Even if you don't fly Alaska or Hawaiian often, the points you earn on the card can help you get outsized value. With a robust network of Oneworld and nonalliance partners, Atmos Rewards can take you just about anywhere in the world. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐.

    *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

    The is a cobranded airline card within Atmos Rewards, the joint loyalty program between Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

    For a $95 annual fee, the card earns valuable Atmos Rewards points and provides a few added benefits.

    Some of the best ways to maximize these points include redeeming for premium cabins with Oneworld partners, such as Cathay Pacific and Fiji Airways. However, Atmos Rewards points are also solid for short-haul domestic routes on Alaska Airlines and American Airlines.

    One of the card's standout perks is its annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) that is earned each account anniversary as long as you've spent $6,000 or more in the prior anniversary year.

    Generally, it's a solid option for Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines frequent flyers, thanks to the perks provided when flying with either airline, such as free checked bags and preferred boarding.

    However, if you're looking for more premium perks like lounge access, this card won't meet your needs.

    Related: Which credit card should you use for Alaska Airlines flights?

    The offers fewer benefits than other cobranded airline cards. However, you can still expect some perks.

    Sources indicate that cardholders receive one piece of free checked luggage for themselves and up to six other passengers on the same reservation when flying Alaska or Hawaiian and paying with the Atmos Rewards Ascent. That can save $45 per person each way on most itineraries, though the first checked bag still costs $30 on intra-Hawaii flights.

    Cardholders also get preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian, and they'll receive 20% back on inflight purchases with both airlines when they use the card.

    If you're working toward Atmos Rewards status, you can earn 1 status point for every $3 spent on the card, with no cap on the number of status points you can earn through spending.

    As mentioned above, one of the best benefits of the Atmos Rewards Ascent is the $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23). This can be unlocked after spending $6,000 or more on the card within the prior anniversary year.

    You'll get value from this perk as long as you fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines with a friend or family member on paid fares at least once a year.

    In a recent development, carly Helfand, TPG's director of content strategy, previously used the Ascent's Companion Fare to take a last-minute trip to Chicago with her husband. The round-trip flights from Portland International Airport (PDX) in Oregon to Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) cost $542.60 per person, but she paid $679.63 for both tickets thanks to the Companion Fare.

    While the Atmos Rewards Ascent doesn't provide outright lounge access, you can get $100 off an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership when you pay with this card. A membership costs $795 per year.

    This benefit alone offsets the card's $95 annual fee. However, given how expensive membership is, this perk isn't too useful unless you were already going to pay for an Alaska Lounge+ membership.

    Recent findings suggest that it's worth noting that this card doesn't provide basic travel protections like baggage delay insurance, lost luggage insurance, purchase protection and trip cancellation/interruption coverage. If these perks are important to you, you may want to consider an alternative option.

    On a more positive note, this is a good card to take abroad since it doesn't charge foreign transaction fees.

    Related: The 5 best airline credit cards with annual fees of $150 or less.

    According to recent reports, the earns Atmos Rewards points on purchases. These points are often best redeemed toward air travel. Let's dive into what to know.

    Plus, cardholders with an eligible Bank of America account will also receive a 10% bonus on all points earned from purchases.

    TPG's November 2026 valuations estimate Atmos Rewards points are worth 1.6 cents apiece.

    This card may not be the best option for spending categories outside of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases. However, if you're all in on earning Atmos Rewards points, swiping this card becomes more attractive.

    Recent findings suggest that atmos Rewards provides stellar redemption rates on domestic travel. Short-haul economy tickets start at just 4,500 points one-way.

    One of my favorite ways to redeem Atmos Rewards points is to book short-haul American Airlines flights, such as Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) to Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport (SDF) in Kentucky, at this 4,500-point rate.

    According to recent reports, it can also be a good deal to redeem for longer domestic flights. For example, a one-way flight from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) starts at 12,500 points in economy.

    Recent findings suggest that premium cabins can start as low as 15,000 points one-way on shorter flights and 30,000 points one-way on longer U.S. routes. For trips to Hawaii, awards from the West Coast typically start at 12,500 points each way in economy and 30,000 points each way in first class.

    Atmos Rewards is part of the Oneworld alliance, which means you can book partner flights with airlines such as British Airways, Cathay Pacific and Qantas. Keep in mind that partner awards include a $20 nonrefundable booking fee.

    Sources indicate that TPG director of travel content Eric Rosen's favorite ways to maximize Atmos Rewards redemptions include booking Cathay Pacific or Japan Airlines business class from the U.S. to Asia for 75,000 points one-way and Fiji Airways business class from the U.S. to Fiji for 75,000 points one-way.

    Related: 10 best ways to redeem 100,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points.

    Despite its benefits, there are a few reasons why you may not want to apply to the $95-annual-fee :.

    If you are ready to go all in on Atmos Rewards, consider its premium sibling: the .

    For a higher $395 annual fee, the card provides eight Alaska Lounge passes each calendar year, a 25,000-point Global Companion Award each account anniversary and a high earning rate on foreign purchases.

    Learn more in our full review of the Atmos Rewards Summit Visa.

    Related: How to reach Alaska Airlines elite status with the Atmos Summit Visa.

    The is a great way to collect valuable Atmos Rewards points. If you value that currency highly, this card is a fantastic starting point.

    However, if you find the earning rates restrictive and the benefits underwhelming, another option may be the best choice.

    Industry observers note that related: Atmos Rewards Ascent vs. Business: Which $95 Alaska-Hawaiian card should you get?

    Recent findings suggest that fresh cardholders can earn 70,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $2,500 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. TPG values this bonus at $1,120, not including the value of the Companion Fare.

    This is a really strong offer, but not the absolute highest we've seen in the card's offer history. Still, it's high enough that I wouldn't hesitate to apply if the timing otherwise makes sense for your personal finances.

    Mexico’s President Spent 21 Hours In Coach Getting To China—And Sat In A Middle Seat

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines.
    • That’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar.
    • Industry observers note that the 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines. She reportedly sat in 33B. A middle seat, on a trip across the Pacific, to represent her country at a summit of world leaders. That’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar. But while Sheinbaum is winning praise for saving taxpayers money, she should have flown business class. The 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Here’s her departure update: Claudia Sheinbaum’s update on her trip to Shenzhen, November 15, 2026 21 Hours Includes The Stop In Tijuana She left Mexico City early Sunday, November 15, on China Southern flight CZ8032 and arrived in Shenzhen on Monday. The Airbus A350-900 made its scheduled technical stop in Tijuana along the way. The first flight took 3 hours 12 minutes and the transpacific segment clocked in at 14 hours 56 minutes, with about two and a half hours on the ground between them. China Southern operates the route nonstop from Shenzhen to Mexico City, with the Tijuana stop in the other direction. Several stories report that seat 33B is in the back of the aircraft. In fact, it’s the front of standard economy. On arrival she posted video of her welcome in Shenzhen. An airport bus brought her to the red carpet, where an honor guard and performers waited. She received a presidential welcome. Which reminds me a little bit of when I’ve booked first class awards on Lufthansa, but the intra-European segment was only available in coach. Nobody ever could quite figure out how a coach passenger had a vehicle waiting for them on the tarmac. She returned on China Southern flight CZ8031 and shared a photo with the crew: Claudia Sheinbaum thanks the crew of flight CZ8031 on her return from Shenzhen Mexico Sold Its Presidential 787 Sheinbaum is continuing a practice established by Andrés Manuel López Obrador. In July 2020, I wrote about Mexico’s president flying Delta coach and connecting in Atlanta to meet Trump. He had an exit row aisle seat on a Delta flight from Mexico City. Delta was blocking middle seats at the time, too, due to the pandemic. Reforma’s video of López Obrador boarding Delta for his Washington trip, July 7, 2020 López Obrador refused to use Mexico’s presidential Boeing 787-8. After years of trying to find a buyer, Mexico sold it to Tajikistan for about $92 million in 2023. He noted the proceeds would fund two hospitals. This isn’t Sheinbaum’s first long trip in coach, either. In April I covered her economy trip to Europe, flying through Madrid to Barcelona and returning to Mexico City on Aeromexico. She posted a photo of herself working at her coach seat: Claudia Sheinbaum working during her April 2026 trip to Barcelona I thought that was performative then. A president’s time has value, and so does being rested for the work the country is sending her to do. Aeromexico business class would have provided better rest and opportunity to work. Pringles, Princes, And A Qatari 747 I’ve covered plenty of politicians and royals flying coach. Prince William flew American Airlines economy from Memphis to Dallas in 2014, in a bulkhead window seat on an Airbus A319. He’s also flown Ryanair and taken the family on Flybe, carrying their hand luggage. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle flew British Airways coach to Nice for Newly introduced Year’s in 2017. They and three bodyguards occupied the last three rows, with empty seats around them. T Argentina’s Javier Milei flew coach on his trip to Davos in January 2024. Given Argentina’s finances and the spending cuts he wanted the public to accept, there was a political purpose for the symbolism. David Cameron was photographed eating Pringles and working on his iPad aboard easyJet in 2015, while traveling to Portugal. I liked that one. William and Harry’s grandfather Prince Philip, though, described the improvements in air travel over his lifetime with the qualification, “provided you don’t travel in something called economy class, which sounds ghastly.” Meanwhile, thhe Pentagon accepted Qatar’s Boeing 747-8 in May 2025 for Trump’s use as Air Force One. It was widely described as a $400 million gift. I covered the Qatari jet’s conversion this summer, including the decision to preserve its luxury interior and the plan for it eventually to go to Trump’s presidential library. The U.S. president needs secure communications, protection, and the ability to keep working while traveling. That can justify dedicated aircraft. Sheinbaum’s coach trip earned publicity, including favorable attention in China while she was there to meet its leaders. But saving the difference between coach and business class is simply a poor value tradeoff when the cost is productive time and sleep for someone with a high opportunity cost.     #111273. Latest Update: An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (952 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: An Overhyped Trilateral Summit

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting.
    • That is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating.
    • Recent findings suggest that the fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “massive three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin have now concluded their first-ever trilateral meeting. Each leader has pronounced himself satisfied with their discussion. But if their concluding statement is an accurate reflection of what was said in the closed session, little of any real consequence — with one possible exception — was agreed to, which was only to be expected. Much has been made by some of the symbolism of the meeting. Did it signal that a disreputable carve-up, even a new Yalta, was underway? If that was the proposal, the result, appropriately and mercifully, looks like a package with more than a touch of Temu about it.

    That is not to deny that some of the optics involved were grating. Trump’s earlier, overly enthusiastic greeting of his “friend” Putin — the aggressor, after all, in a genocidal war — was not only nauseating but also careless. It sent a disturbing signal to the rest of NATO, an organization that still plays a critical role in maintaining American security as well as peace, however uneasy, in Europe west of Ukraine. It is to be hoped that Trump’s delight at the sight of his supposed pal was, to use a word often applied to this president’s approach to diplomacy, transactional, a display of a dealmaker’s schmooze and nothing more.

    Recent findings suggest that the fact that Putin was in the room has attracted criticism for its symbolic “confirmation” of Russia as one of, to borrow a term from the real Yalta, the “massive three.” Not so much: Putin’s presence merely reflected geopolitical reality, something that, however unpleasant, cannot be wished away. Russia is economically enfeebled and embroiled in a brutally and humiliatingly debilitating war, but it remains a vast, resource-rich country that, militarily anyway, counts as a superpower and one that, as Ukrainians can testify, is still capable of wreaking immense destruction. The more interesting symbolism was detectable in the various gestures through which Xi Jinping emphasized during Putin’s visit that Russia is China’s junior partner. That, too, is today’s reality.

    It has been revealed that as alluded to above, the joint statement issued after the meeting was, as should have been expected, thin gruel. There was talk of reforming the U.N. “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its fundamental mission of maintaining international peace and security.” If that implies reining in Turtle Bay’s efforts to extend supranational (and thus post-democratic) governance, that’s no bad thing, but in practice little will probably change.

    Industry observers note that in a similar vein, the trio, whose countries have not submitted to the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, implicitly criticized the attempted extension of its reach. They stressed the need for “respect for immunities of State officials,” a subject doubtless close to Putin’s heart. There is no need to grumble too much about this. The ICC is highly politicized, and, while it does not constitute much of a deterrent, it may even provide a perverse incentive to wrongdoers to hang onto power. Putin deserves to face judgment, but a better place for that would be Kyiv, not The Hague.

    And all three declared that they planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” If that reflected some post-midterms unease on Trump’s part, that, as an admission of weakness, would have been a message better not sent. It would also be a mistake, despite recent waivers, for the U.S. to abandon its general application of sanctions on Iranian and Russian oil (the Europeans, incidentally, could do a better job of enforcing theirs). No pressure should be put on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure other than as part of a general “energy cease-fire” such as that floated earlier this year, which Ukraine was willing to accept.

    No details have been released so far of what was said in the meeting about Ukraine. However, Putin has been reiterating his hard line, supplemented by an absurd and aggressive proposal to rewrite Europe’s security architecture. Hopefully, Trump was not misled by any bonhomie in Shenzhen, although some accounts of his later call with European leaders were not entirely encouraging in that respect.

    Industry observers note that from left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump participate in a trilateral meeting during the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.

    In a recent development, to return to reality: China has no interest in helping end the war in Ukraine, and Russia’s ambitions in Europe are such that the eventual consequences of undermining Kyiv’s ability to resist won’t stop at Ukraine’s borders. Speaking of which, we hope that Trump warned Xi and Putin that the growing intensity of “gray zone” activity, from drones in Leipzig Airport to cyberattacks on both sides of the Atlantic, risks triggering retaliation that could easily spiral into something extremely dangerous.

    Any claims that the Shenzhen meeting has delivered the death blow to the post-1945 order would be overblown, akin to complaining about the murder of a corpse. The postwar settlement has been in flux for decades — Nixon, after all, went to China — a process that has accelerated, along with dramatic shifts in relative global economic and political power, since the Soviet collapse. But although the landscape has changed, Trump should pay more attention to America’s successful management of the (first) Cold War. Alliances matter, deterrence works, strength is rewarded, and aggression by, or sponsored by, hostile powers and their proxies should be contained and, where possible, reversed.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    • This incident happened on the morning of Saturday, November 21, 2026, and involves Alaska Airlines flight AS1306, scheduled to operate from Seattle (SEA) to Los Angeles (LAX).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An Alaska Airlines flight was delayed by hours after masked ICE agents stormed the jet bridge of a departing flight to arrest a Mexican national who allegedly had a work permit had overstayed his visa (you know, “the worst of the worst”). This ended up turning into a huge jet bridge melee, leading to additional arrests, as ICE claims that someone hurled hot coffee at the officers.

    Recent findings suggest that in the end, the flight was delayed by hours, as the crew was no longer fit to fly, and the Port of Seattle is outraged. This is quite the story, as flagged by PYOK.

    This incident happened on the morning of Saturday, November 21, 2026, and involves Alaska Airlines flight AS1306, scheduled to operate from Seattle (SEA) to Los Angeles (LAX).

    This was first reported by a passenger on the flight, who explained that “ICE agents just arrested multiple people at SeaTac Airport inside the jet bridge as we were all boarding,” and went on to explain that they were “deplaning because the crew is being replaced due to poor morale.”.

    ICE agents just arrested multiple people at SeaTac Airport inside the jet bridge as we were all boarding. Now deplaning because the crew is being replaced due to poor morale @CNN @nytimes @seattletimes.

    Video taken from the jet bridge demonstrates masked ICE agents trying to arrest people on the jet bridge.

    Masked ICE agents detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as passengers were boarding a flight. Alaska Airlines stated ICE officers gave them no advance notice of the operation. pic.twitter.com/r44WPTvGdv.

    It has been revealed that as a result of this incident, the Alaska flight ended up being delayed by hours. It was initially supposed to depart at 8:10AM and arrive at 11:01AM, but instead, departed at 11:03AM and arrived at 1:36PM.

    Here’s how ICE explained its actions:.

    According to recent reports, on November 21, 2026, at approximately 8:05 a.m. PST, ICE officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.

    During the arrest other travelers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers—a federal crime and a felony. One passenger hurled hot coffee on the officers. Other passengers began obstructing federal officers.

    The individual who threw the hot coffee was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay. She was subsequently arrested as well. She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

    According to recent reports, assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime and a felony. Secretary Mullin has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the fullest extent of the law. Our brave law enforcement is facing more than a 1,600% increase in assaults, 3,300% increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats against them. This violence must end.

    On November 21, 2026, at approximately 8:05 a.m. PST, ICE officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws. During the arrest other travelers began to… https://t.co/nXiBxAqIJ5.

    The Port of Seattle expressed its outrage about the incident, releasing the following statement:.

    It has been revealed that we are outraged about this morning’s incident involving ICE and two passengers as travelers boarded AS 1306 to Los Angeles. Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge. The Port has continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS on whether any of these protocols were breached. However, the Port remains committed to the safety of all of our travelers and staff and airline team. This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.

    Washington Governor Bob Ferguson was also angry, as he held a press conference about what happened, and released the following statement:.

    ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities. Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics. I’ll have more to say this afternoon.

    Meanwhile Alaska Airlines took a more toned down approach, and just expressed “concern,” releasing the following statement:.

    Recent findings suggest that we are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306. We recognize how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests. Alaska Airlines is required to comply with applicable laws and regulations when interacting with law enforcement officials. We do not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity, and we remain committed to protecting the privacy and safety of our guests and employees wherever possible.

    There’s simply no arguing that in terms of public sentiment, the tides have turned in terms of immigration enforcement, with even Trump recently admitting “I think it might be too tough.”.

    Recent findings suggest that Q: You think your deportation policy went too far?Trump: I think it might be too tough. pic.twitter.com/NKhFjZKxnd.

    According to recent reports, no matter how you feel about deportations as such, having them go down in this way for someone who simply overstayed their visa is a step too far, in my opinion. I mean, it’s one thing if we’re talking about a violent criminal on some sort of watch list, but that’s clearly not the case here.

    Our four-year-old is currently at the age where he asks “why” in response to everything… and he has a lot of good questions that often make me step back and think “oh, that’s a good point.” I put myself in the situation of being on the jet bridge here as a parent, and trying to explain what was going on.

    And here’s the thing — it’s one thing if these people were in uniform and identifying themselves, but when you have people who refuse to identify themselves, it’s an especially bad look. It reminds me of another incident we recently saw at Las Vegas Airport (LAS). Like, is this person being robbed in the terminal, or is this an official law enforcement operation?

    A post shared by Chris Motley (@motleymodel).

    It has been revealed that on Saturday, an Alaska Airlines flight was delayed by a few hours after ICE agents stormed a jet bridge to arrest someone, leading to a larger fight, which also caused more arrests. It’s one thing if such a disruptive operation were targeting a violent criminal, but is this really the way that someone who overstays a visa should be apprehended?

    The Port of Seattle has expressed outrage over how this was handled, while ICE is outraged at how its “brave law enforcement” is facing increasing violence from the public.

    #111270. JSX Buys Latest Pacific Airlines—42 Seat Jets Could Bring Its Private Terminal Flights To More Travelers

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2360 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    JSX Buys Latest Pacific Airlines—42 Seat Jets Could Bring Its Private Terminal Flights To More Travelers

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, JSX has acquired New Pacific Airlines, and prepares to bring the failed airline back with 42 seat Embraer regional jets.
    • Sources indicate that I think this fits a manufacturer that’s been unusually creative about finding markets and figuring out how to serve them.
    • JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more Customers and more communities.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, JSX has acquired New Pacific Airlines, and prepares to bring the failed airline back with 42 seat Embraer regional jets. That’s 12 more seats than JSX sells on its planes today, and it gives them a way to grow beyond the limits of their current operation. I think this fits a company that’s been unusually creative about finding markets and figuring out how to serve them. They brought turboprops to Santa Monica’s shortened runway and used a free membership program to gain access to Teterboro in order to serve New York. JSX isn’t laying out the New Pacific strategy yet. Asked about the deal, they tell me: JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more Customers and more communities. As part of that work, we are pursuing additional pathways that could provide even more ways to deliver our award-winning service in the future. Our focus remains on the exceptional experience, convenience, and hospitality our Customers have come to expect from JSX. New Pacific has filed its intent to resume flying and requested a waiver of the usual 45 day advance filing requirement. An operating projection calls for: Embraer ERJ145-LR aircraft with 42 seats. Two aircraft initially, growing to six by the fifth month. 10,106 flights and roughly 309,000 passenger boardings in the first year. Flights averaging about 1.2 hours gate to gate, with staffing growing to 104 employees. New Pacific used to be Northern Pacific, the startup that wanted to connect the mainland U.S. and Asia through Anchorage using Boeing 757s. It seemed unlikely to work anyway but the closure of Russian airspace to U.S. carriers kept them from even trying. It pivoted to short domestic routes and then sports and corporate charters. I reported its shutdown last November, just two weeks after it announced an all-business class venture with beOnd. The bankruptcy process disposed of its 757s. What it has instead is Part 121 certification allowing operations beyond the 30 passenger limit of JSX’s current Part 135 public charter model. I first flew JSX home from Southwest Airlines Media Day in late 2022. JSX’s 4 p.m. departure got me home for dinner, an hour ahead of the Southwest flight I would have taken. I reached the terminal 19 minutes before departure. In Austin, I was in a Lyft less than ten minutes after touchdown. The plane was comfortable, with a seat on each side of the aisle and a side table next to mine. But getting my time back was what made it worth paying more (but honestly, not much more). I didn’t need a bigger airport lounge. I needed to spend less time at the airport. By my March 2023 visit to JSX’s headquarters, they’d fixed my one real complaint: no internet. JSX was the first carrier with Starlink, and the first to finish equipping its full fleet. Notably United Airlines owns a stake in JSX. The early JSX adoption is likely related to United’s head start with Starlink among major airlines. JSX’s business depended on putting several things together: inexpensive used aircraft, a comfortable cabin, friendly service and airports that let customers avoid wasting time. At the time, airport real estate was their biggest constraint. Finding another city with people willing to buy a ticket wasn’t enough. They needed somewhere to put the operation. Look at Santa Monica. The city is literally closing the airport and shortened its runway to 3,500 feet. JSX brought in ATR 42-600 turboprops configured with 30 seats. They found an aircraft suited to an airport that’s convenient for customers on the west side of Los Angeles, and obtained permission to operate despite the local politics. At Teterboro, the solution involved how they sold tickets. The airport prohibits publicly advertised scheduled passenger service. JSX put the flights behind a Club JSX login, limited bookings to members, and marketed the destination publicly as New York City. Joining the program is free, but joining is how they gain access to the airport. Those are different solutions to different problems. With New Pacific, JSX gains the ability to operate with more than 30 seats. My guess is that they see markets where a different version of their product could work, with more passengers sharing the cost of each departure. There is a regulatory insurance benefit. American Airlines, Southwest and the big pilots union have pushed to restrict JSX’s business model. I anticipated that sort of campaign in my first review. Having a Part 121 operation would be useful if the rules change. But the Federal Aviation Administration’s current agenda lists its public charter rulemaking as a long-term action with the next step undetermined. They never closed the rulemaking effort. But I think it’s possible to overread the regulatory risk insurance strategy here. They could still use private terminals with a part 121 operation and 42 seats. Federal security rules provide for scheduled and public charter flights with 31 to 60 seats outside the usual secure terminal area. This wouldn’t work at every airport JSX currently serves due to airport certification requirements. And part 121 means different pilot requirements, including mandatory age 65 retirement (they couldn’t use their ex-American and Southwest senior captains). If they do blueprint 42 seats that a different product – still more generous than a 50-seat sardine can but not nearly as spacious as the current 30-seat setup JSX appears to have a plan to add 40% more seats to some of the regional jets they own, and operate them under a scheduled airline. They haven’t said what they’re actually planning, but it may be a different niche than their current model rather than the assumed ‘buy a scheduled airline in case the next administration capitulates to lobbyists and puts them out of business’ the way ALPA, Southwest and American sought to do under the last administration.     Those are different solutions to different problems. With Newly introduced Pacific, JSX gains the ability to operate with more than 30 seats. My guess is that they see markets where a different version of their product could work, with more passengers sharing the cost of each departure.

    There is a regulatory insurance benefit. American Airlines, Southwest and the big pilots union have pushed to restrict JSX’s business model. I anticipated that sort of campaign in my first review. Having a Part 121 operation would be useful if the rules change. But the Federal Aviation Administration’s current agenda lists its public charter rulemaking as a long-term action with the next step undetermined. They never closed the rulemaking effort. But I think it’s possible to overread the regulatory risk insurance strategy here.

    They could still use private terminals with a part 121 operation and 42 seats. Federal security rules provide for scheduled and public charter flights with 31 to 60 seats outside the usual secure terminal area.

    This wouldn’t work at every airport JSX currently serves due to airport certification requirements. And part 121 means different pilot requirements, including mandatory age 65 retirement (they couldn’t use their ex-American and Southwest senior captains).

    The Week: The Three Amigos Summit

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (241 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • • We swear, it wasn’t our redesigned website that brought down email and the airlines.
    • • In an unprecedented trilateral summit in China this week, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat down with President Donald Trump.
    • NR Editors includes members of the editorial staff of our magazine and website.

    • We swear, it wasn’t our redesigned website that brought down email and the airlines.

    • In an unprecedented trilateral summit in China this week, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat down with President Donald Trump. Ahead of the summit, Trump set no metrics for observers to judge its success. The summit cannot be said to have failed: It was not designed to achieve anything, and it didn’t. Of course, the president reportedly went into the diplomatic event of the year with some goals in mind. He reportedly sought commitments to nuclear disarmament from his Russian and Chinese counterparts, neither of whom had an incentive to agree to such limits. If Trump persuaded them to assist America’s efforts to isolate Iran economically, he has kept it a closely guarded secret. Putin sought to make the summit all about his war on Ukraine, but the Russian autocrat secured no meaningful promises on that front from Washington or Beijing. Only China, it seems, got what it wanted from the summit, which took place on its soil. The event allowed Xi to pretend to arbitrate the conflicts in which his great-power competitors are embroiled. The affair was not entirely unproductive, of course. It produced many joint statements of principle, which essentially state that all parties have agreed to keep talking.

    NR Editors includes members of the editorial staff of our magazine and website.

    On “The Week: The Three Amigos Summit”.

    #111267. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1416 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov.
    • Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    According to recent reports, “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting noted the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    Recent findings suggest that that was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., stated Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    Industry observers note that “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday noted at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    According to recent reports, but there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    Sources indicate that “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., mentioned Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the fresh ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    Sources indicate that several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who stated he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    It has been revealed that kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    In a recent development, “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he remarked. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but remarked, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    In a recent development, “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he mentioned. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for newly introduced leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    According to recent reports, “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan noted.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    In a recent development, sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., stated, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    #111266. United Nigeria Airlines Flew Passengers To The Wrong City—3 Years Later, Chairman Admits They Lied About It

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2264 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    United Nigeria Airlines Flew Passengers To The Wrong City—3 Years Later, Chairman Admits They Lied About It

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, united Nigeria Airlines flew passengers to the wrong city and blamed the weather.
    • It has been revealed that I covered this incident on November 28, 2023, including the conflict between the pilot reportedly acknowledging a wrong flight strategy and the airline insisting on a weather diversion.
    • It has been revealed that executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo revisited the episode at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, united Nigeria Airlines flew passengers to the wrong city and blamed the weather. Three years later, they’re admitting it was all a lie. I covered this incident on November 28, 2023, including the conflict between the pilot reportedly acknowledging a wrong flight initiative and the airline insisting on a weather diversion. Now, Live and Let’s Fly flags the airline chairman’s admission that the passengers’ explanation was right. Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo revisited the episode at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17. A dispatcher had entered the wrong destination in the paperwork. The pilots flew there. The flight attendants apparently believed they’d reached the city everyone bought tickets to. He described the weather explanation as “just a lie” and offered this advice: “The best way of public relations is to tell the truth, but tell it responsibly.” Passengers Were Welcomed To Abuja While Sitting In Asaba On November 26, 2023, flight 0504 left Lagos with passengers booked to Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. It landed in Asaba instead, about 200 miles away. This was United Nigeria Airlines, not United Airlines. Passengers reported that the flight attendants welcomed everyone to Abuja but then everyone discovered where they actually were. November 26, 2023 — Peacock (@dawisu) Another passenger shared video: We legit got scared sha. Laff wan kee me 😅 pic.twitter.com/sWxbnJeDna— Lord Macky (@AugustineMacky) November 26, 2023 The airline’s original statement blamed “poor destination weather”, remarked the pilot knew about the diversion, and attributed the confusion to an incorrect cabin announcement. The plane eventually continued to Abuja. The Investigation Uncovered The Truth The flight used an Airbus A320 operated by Bulgaria’s Fly2Sky for United Nigeria Airlines. Fly2Sky said at the time that United Nigeria had assigned it a Lagos–Asaba flight the previous day and hadn’t requested a change during the pilots’ preflight briefing. The Nigerian regulator identified failures well beyond one person entering a destination incorrectly. In its findings there was: Poor coordination between United Nigeria’s operations center and the firm supplying the aircraft. No joint preflight briefing between the pilots and flight attendants. United Nigeria’s failure to monitor the leased aircraft through its operations center. Failure to follow the approved flight plan filed with air traffic control. The chairman story is about a dispatch error. The regulator, though, laid out several opportunities to prevent it. British Airways Has Done It, Too In March 2019, a British Airways flight scheduled from London City to Düsseldorf went to Edinburgh after the pilots received paperwork for the wrong destination. The passengers had bought a flight to Germany but the flight took them to Scotland. A few weeks later, Scandinavian Airlines sent a Copenhagen–Florence flight to Bologna. That was a deliberate decision made before departure because the pilots lacked the correct routing information for Florence. They flew to Bologna with plans to bus passengers onward. It’s just that they kept this information to themselves. And in August 2025, I covered AirAsia X passengers being welcomed to Incheon after their Kuala Lumpur flight landed at Seoul’s Gimpo airport, about 20 miles away. Here’s the Instagram video from that coverage: View the video shared by @rizalhakimm_punyer on Instagram AirAsia X said it had intentionally diverted for fuel because bad weather had caused congestion at Incheon. It acknowledged an incorrect cabin announcement, said the captain corrected it, and offered travel vouchers. Okonkwo also used his conference appearance to discuss a passenger upset that an advertised 11:30 a.m. flight had left at 11:20. He said he’d initially wanted to shout back, but instead responded, “I apologise for United Nigeria Airline leaving on time.” An airline chairman giving a speech about accurately convey what on-time means.     Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, former Alaska Rep.
    • In a recent development, former Rep.
    • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    In a recent development, former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

    According to recent reports, the Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    According to recent reports, she entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    Sources indicate that but the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

    In a recent development, prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Recent findings suggest that trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    It has been revealed that "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer noted in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    According to recent reports, in other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

Her charges break down as: Six felonies: three counts of battery on a law enforcement officer, one count of resisting an officer with violence, and two counts of controlled substance possession involving the Adderall and THC oil. Three misdemeanors: disorderly intoxication, resisting an officer without violence, and possession of less than 20 grams of cannabis. She was booked at 5:21 p.m. on November 8. At her first appearance the next day, the court set bonds totaling $26,150. After two nights in jail, she was released November 10 on bond.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that on the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”.

    “When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump stated, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”.

    “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”.

    The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the Upcoming York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the Newly introduced York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how significant a role early votes will play in the outcome.
